The iPhone Air also starts in a 256GB configuration, costing $1,099 / £1,099 / AU$1,899, while the 512GB model is $1,299 / £1,299 / AU$2,299, and the 1TB version is $1,699 / £1,699 / AU$3,099. There’s no 2TB version of this phone.
So, the iPhone Duo’s starting price is some $900 / £900 / AU$1,600 higher than the iPhone Air’s, and to be honest, you're unlikely to need to pay full price for Apple's super slim handset. It's regularly on sale at third-party retailers including Amazon, so the price gap between it and the iPhone Duo is $900 / £900 / AU$1,600 at worst.
With the money you’d be saving by buying the Air, you could also buy an iPhone 17 or an iPad Air, which speaks to how expensive Apple's first foldable phone is.

| 1TB | $1,699 | £1,699 | AU$3,099 | 
iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: design
Both of these phones are, first and foremost, examples of beautiful design.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple managed to make a remarkably slim phone that’s just 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm when unfolded. That makes it even thinner than the 156.2 x 74.7 x 5.6mm iPhone Air — a phone that has a slim design as one of its main selling points.
Of course, when folded shut — as it will be in your pocket — the iPhone Duo is rather chunkier at 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm. At 254g, the Duo also weighs a lot more than the Air, which clocks in at a remarkably light 165g.
Before we move on, it's worth reiterating that these measurements make the Air one of the most comfortable phones to use and hold over long periods. Its slimness might seem like a gimmick, but there's a lot to be said for using a phone that feels almost weightless in your hand and pocket.
The Duo is equally well-crafted and impressively thin when unfolded, but in day-to-day use, it feels significantly heavier and chunkier than the Air. But then, with two screens, that was inevitable.
As far as durability goes, both phones have a Ceramic Shield 2 glass front, a Ceramic Shield glass back, and a titanium frame, and both also have an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance.
Of course, foldables are inherently more fragile than single-screen phones like the iPhone Air, but you needn't worry about the Duo breaking after a few folds — Apple has confirmed to TechRadar that the phone's viral screen-cracking issue only affected a "small number of units" at launch.
The iPhone Duo and iPhone Air also look somewhat similar from the back, with both having a horizontal camera block — though this block houses two lenses on the iPhone Duo, and just one on the iPhone Air.
On the front, the Air has larger cutouts in its screen, allowing for Face ID — something the iPhone Duo lacks. And the two phones come in different colors, with the iPhone Duo being available in Night Sky and Star White shades, while the iPhone Air is sold in Space Black, Cloud White, Light Gold, and Sky Blue shades.
So, there are as many differences as similarities here, but the designs of both phones shine, with our iPhone Duo review praising Apple's foldable as “beautifully designed and engineered,” while our iPhone Air review called it “the freshest look that Apple has delivered in years.” These are two great-looking products.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: display
You may not have noticed, but the iPhone Duo has two screens.
Its main foldable display is a 7.6-inch 1878 x 2670 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel with 430 pixels per inch, a 120Hz refresh rate, a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, and an anti-glare nano-texture finish.
Its smaller cover screen is a 5.4-inch 1398 x 2034 LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED panel with 60 pixels per inch, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a peak brightness of 3,000 nits.
The iPhone Air, of course, just has one screen — a 6.5-inch 1260 x 2736 Super Retina XDR OLED panel with 460 pixels per inch, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a peak brightness of 3,000 nits.
The specs and quality of both phones' front screens are similar, with our iPhone Duo review saying it has a “bright, sharp, fluid display,” and our iPhone Air review calling its screen “punchy, sharp, and smooth.” So you’re mostly just choosing whether you want one screen or two, and what size(s) you want.
That said, having two displays undeniably makes the iPhone Duo more versatile, as it’s suited to both large-screen and small-screen tasks — it also supports the Apple Pencil, which the iPhone Air doesn’t.
The nano-texture finish on the Duo's inner screen is a sight to behold, too. It does an excellent job of preventing glare, and an even better job of hiding the phone's crease when viewed straight-on. This crease is, of course, still visible when viewed at an angle, but that doesn't really matter if it's not visible when the Duo is in use.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: cameras
iPhones tend to excel at photography, but arguably neither of these devices ranks among Apple’s best. Still, of the two, the iPhone Duo has the edge by virtue of having more cameras.
On the back, it has a 48MP f/1.6 wide camera and a 48MP f/2.2 ultra-wide one (with a 120-degree field of view). Then, on the cover screen, it has a 12MP f/2.2 punch-hole camera, and on the foldable screen, it has a 4MP f/1.8 under-display one.
The iPhone Air, on the other hand, has a solitary 48 MP f/1.6 wide camera on the back, and an 18MP f/1.9 camera on the front.
So the main difference here is that there’s no ultra-wide lens on the iPhone Air, making the Duo more versatile for photography. But the Air does have a superior selfie camera, even if the Duo has two front-facing snappers (the 4MP inner-display camera is really not very good).
All that said, both phones are still capable ot taking excellent shots. In our iPhone Duo review, we said it has “two strong 48MP lenses and an above-average Center Stage selfie camera,” while in our iPhone Air review, we said its camera “delivers sharp, natural photos and impressive portraits, but lacks the versatility found on other models.”

iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: performance and software
The iPhone Duo has an A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, and a vapor chamber, putting it in line with the performance of the iPhone 18 Pro series. The iPhone Air is a step down from that, with an A19 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, and no vapor chamber.
As such, the Air isn’t quite as high-performing, though unless you’re really pushing it with high-end games or other demanding tasks, you’re unlikely to notice much of a difference, and both phones are speedy.
This was reflected in our use of the two devices, with our iPhone Duo review finding that it offered “smooth performance across the board,” while our iPhone Air review said it “feels fast and smooth in daily use, though it can warm up under sustained heavy gaming.” The Air occasionally heats up during FaceTime calls, too.
As for software, the iPhone Duo launched with iOS 27.1 out of the box, while the iPhone Air — being older — shipped with iOS 26. But both phones can be updated to iOS 27.2 at the time of writing, so there’s not much to choose between them here, though the Duo does feature some unique touches like a side-positioned dock.
However, it’s worth noting that it might take a while for all apps to be optimized for the iPhone Duo’s form factor. First-party apps like Messages and Mail look great on either Duo screen, but third-party apps like YouTube and Instagram still need work.
This early-stage clunkiness may well be resolved by the time you're reading this, but don't be surprised if you encounter some software-related oddities on the iPhone Duo.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: battery
The iPhone Duo has a 4,883mAh battery, while the iPhone Air has a far lower-capacity 3,149mAh cell. This, unsurprisingly, also means the iPhone Duo lasts longer, with Apple claiming you’ll get 44 hours of video playback from it when using the cover screen or 31 hours with the foldable display, while the iPhone Air is quoted at 27 hours.
This largely tallies with our test results. In the case of the iPhone Duo, our reviewer found that “all-day battery life is virtually assured,” while for the iPhone Air we found that it “should last a workday, but heavy users will need to recharge.”
And when you do recharge, the iPhone Duo can reach 50% in roughly 20 minutes with a 60W or higher charger, or if you’re using wireless charging, it can get to 50% in around 30 minutes with a 35W or higher MagSafe charger.
The iPhone Air takes about 30 minutes to reach a 50% charge whether using wired or wireless charging, so it’s slightly slower here.
iPhone Duo vs iPhone Air: verdict
The iPhone Duo is far more expensive than the iPhone Air, and that price difference is probably the main thing you need to consider when choosing between them — especially as you could buy the iPhone Air and an iPad for less money than the iPhone Duo.
Of course, there are advantages to having two devices in one, and the iPhone Duo is a better phone than the Air in various ways too — it boasts slightly better performance, longer battery life, an extra camera, and, of course, that all-important second screen.
Both phones have sumptuous designs, though, and the iPhone Air can hold its own for screen quality — it also features Face ID, which the iPhone Duo lacks.
So, if you want a more affordable, beautiful-to-use iPhone that works like every other iPhone you've ever owned, go for the Air. If you're willing to try something new — and happy to pay for the privilege of doing so — the Duo is the obvious choice.

James is a freelance phones, tablets and wearables writer and sub-editor at TechRadar. He has a love for everything ‘smart’, from watches to lights, and can often be found arguing with AI assistants or drowning in the latest apps. James also contributes to 3G.co.uk, 4G.co.uk and 5G.co.uk and has written for T3, Digital Camera World, Clarity Media and others, with work on the web, in print and on TV.

articles.title: Cuál es el valor en el mercado de la criptomoneda Bitcoin este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
Mientras el debate se acalora cada día más sobre la conveniencia o no de su uso, bitcoin cotiza este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) en 77830.78 USD, lo que supone un cambio de 0.55% con respecto a las últimas 24 horas y una variación de 0.0% con referencia a su valor alcanzado en la última hora.
En cuanto a su capitalización de mercado, ha mantenido el puesto #1 entre las monedas digitales.
Bitcoin alcanzó su máximo histórico
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: I test over a dozen coffee makers a year, and these 3 non-toxic machines are my top recommendations if you're looking for great taste without BPA
articles.text:
Looking for a non-toxic coffee maker? I'm a certified barista, and these are my top 3 BPA-free picks for great taste and peace of mind
Looking for a non-toxic coffee maker? I test over a dozen espresso and drip coffee machines every year, and here I've picked out three BPA-free options that deliver peace of mind when you're enjoying your morning brew.
Bisphenol A (BPA) is a material used in some hard plastics, and is classified as an endocrine disruptor (a substance that can affect hormone levels). When it comes into contact with food and drinks, tiny amounts can be transferred and consumed.
The official stance of the US Food and Drink Administration (FDA) is that "BPA is safe at the current levels occurring in foods. Based on FDA’s ongoing safety review of scientific evidence, the available information continues to support the safety of BPA for the currently approved uses in food containers and packaging."
The Food Standards Agency in the UK adopts a similar position, stating that "Where it is allowed to be used, tiny amounts of the chemical may be transferred from some packaging into food and drinks, however the level of BPA detected in food to date in the UK is not currently considered to be harmful."
However, in both countries BPAs are forbidden in items intended to be used by babies and young children, and some coffee fans prefer to pick brewers that are BPA-free to play it safe.
All three coffee makers below are explicitly marked as BPA-free, but there are some other options to consider if you want to avoid contact with plastics. For example, if you want a manual espresso machine, the La Pavoni Europiccola (reviewed by my colleague Josephine Watson) is worth a look. Although it isn't explicitly marketed as non-toxic, the heating element is stainless steel, and its tank is made from brass to limit contact with other materials in the brew path. Meanwhile, pour-over fans can avoid plastic entirely by opting for a Chemex brewer, or a simple glass or ceramic dripper.
Ninja Prestige DualBrew System

The Ninja Prestige DualBrew System — known as the Ninja Espresso and Coffee Maker Barista System in the US — is BPA-free, plus Ninja's product FAQ also states that it's free from PTFE/PFOA, chemicals used to make non-stick coatings. PTFE is chemically inert, and regarded as safe at the temperatures used by coffee machines. However, as with BPAs, some coffee-drinkers prefer to avoid it for peace of mind. PFOA has been phased out in the US and UK, having been classified as carcinogenic by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. You will not find it in any modern coffee makers.

The Prestige DualBrew System was released two years ago, but remains one of my favorite two-in-one coffee and espresso machines for sluggish mornings. Either fill the brew basket with ground coffee before bed, set the timer, and wake to a hot pitcher full of delicious pour-over, or drop in a Nespresso Original pod and enjoy a rich espresso with zero effort.
It's the little features that really make the DualBrew System stand out. For example, the hotplate under the pour-over pitcher offers adjustable time and temperature settings, so you can keep your coffee pleasantly warm without risk of stewing it. Remove the pitcher and you'll find a fold-down drip tray, so you can dispense coffee directly into a cup or travel mug instead.
You can adjust the height of the espresso drip tray to accommodate different-sized cups, too, and around the side of the machine, there's a fold-out milk frother for turning your Nespresso drinks into lattes or cappuccinos. It doesn't heat the milk as a steam wand would, but Ninja's designers have added a "recipe" label that provides guidance on the length of time for which you should microwave and whisk the milk for different drinks.

Ninja Luxe Café Premier
The Luxe Café Premier (which was known as the Luxe Café when it launched in 2024) is another Ninja coffee maker explicitly stated to be BPA-free. Ninja also notes that "after the reservoir, the water does not come into contact with any plastic," which is good to know if you're worried about substances leaching into hot water.
It's a brilliant all-in-one coffee maker that takes the trial and error out of making well-extracted coffee, handling the trickiest barista tasks and helping even first-time users produce a consistently well-extracted brew with a fully rounded flavor.
When preparing an espresso, the machine does the hard work of dialing in the grinder for you, suggesting an appropriate grind size and then funneling the prepared coffee neatly into the filter basket. A calibrated tamper helps you create a perfectly even bed of coffee, and once the handle is inserted under the brewing group, the Luxe Café will time your shot to make sure it's not extracting too fast or slow.
You can push the steam wand down into your milk jug to use the automatic frothing system, or lift it a few degrees to use it manually, depending on how confident you feel. We found that the auto system worked equally well with dairy milk and plant-based substitutes such as oat and almond.
"Overall, the Ninja Luxe Café delivered on its promises of uncomplicating espresso," said our tester Danielle Abraham. "It consistently created quality espresso and made things simpler by intuitively dosing and providing the correct grind level for the perfect pull, something you’d be hard-pressed to find on other semi-automatic espresso machines at this price point."
If you have a small kitchen, the Ninja Luxe Café Mini offers almost exactly the same features in a more compact package, brews "absolutely delicious" coffee, and is also BPA-free.
Read our full Ninja Luxe Café Premier review
Fellow Aiden Precision Coffee Maker

Fellow's premium coffee makers are a popular choice for coffee roasters and specialty cafés, and the Aiden Precision Coffee Maker is no exception. The brand states that "Aiden is built with high-quality, food-grade plastic (BPA-free), stainless steel, and silicone, so that you can brew with peace of mind."
The Aiden offers a choice of brewing modes, so you can pick the appropriate one depending on how much time you have to spare. Auto Brew mode works like any basic drip coffee maker, simply heating water and pumping it over your ground coffee. The pump will run until the water tank is empty.
Guided Brewing mode is where things get interesting. It lets you choose how much to brew, then suggests the optimal dosage, bloom time, and temperature based on the type of beans you've selected. The machine will also tell you whether to use the cone or flat-bottomed brew basket, and can detect which one you've inserted.
The Aiden has a cold-brew mode as well, which uses hot water to bloom the coffee, then switches to cold for the remainder of the process. It's a clever trick that means your drink takes just 1.5-2 hours to prepare compared to the 24 hours for traditional cold brewing. The flavor profile is impressively similar, so hats off to Fellow.
However, the Aiden loses half a point for its carafe, which lets heat escape a little too easily. Fellow claims it will keep your batch of freshly brewed coffee hot for hours, but during my tests, it cooled noticeably within 45 minutes.
In short, the non-toxic Aiden brews exquisite drip coffee, but you'll need to be ready to enjoy it straight away.

articles.title: Cómo ha cambiado el valor de la criptomoneda ethereum en el último día
articles.text:
Ethereum es una plataforma digital que adopta la tecnología de cadena de bloques (blockchain) y expande su uso a una gran variedad de aplicaciones, mientras que ether es su criptomoneda nativa. En el mundo de las finanzas digitales es común que la criptomoneda sea llamada como la red, aunque en realidad no son lo mismo.
La plataforma ethereum, creada en el 2015 por el programador Vitalik Buterin, buscaba ser un instrumento para aplicaciones descentralizadas y colaborativas sobre las que se pueden hacer contratos inteligentes (dAPPs)
Al igual que el bitcoin, el valor de ether se disparó en un corto periodo de tiempo. En enero de 2016, ether cotizaba alrededor de un dólar y actualmente tiene un máximo histórico de 4.953,73 dólares.
El costo de la criptomoneda ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2264.93 dólares. Esto quiere decir que el activo digital reportó un cambio de 0.83% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #2 entre las más populares.
Valor de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: 'AI is not creating the problem': OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says AI is merely uncovering all the vulnerabilities we've accumulated over the years
articles.text:
'AI is not creating the problem': OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says AI is merely uncovering all the vulnerabilities we've accumulated over the years
We need to change how we address security fixes, Altman says
- Sam Altman says AI isn't creating security vulnerabilities – it's just helping us discover them far more quickly
- Attackers are also finding and exploiting them just as quickly
- AI Security Mesh helps you explore fixes at a faster pace
"AI is helping us discover all of the security issues that we have developed over the past fifty years," co-CEO Clay Magouyrk worked into a conversation on-stage with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, clearly laboring the point that artificial intelligence is actually helping us to identify existing vulnerabilities.
This comes against a backdrop of what could only be described as an onslaught of AI-assisted bug patches – companies are now patching at rates we've never seen before. Oracle's own quarterly patch update recently addressed no fewer than around 3,000 issues, most of which were only identified thanks to AI.
With this in mind, Oracle is now helping businesses identify vulnerabilities, investigate exploits before they happen and research fixes through a new partnership with OpenAI.
AI is uncovering thousands of existing vulnerabilities
With the new Oracle AI Security Mesh feature, businesses will be able to see supporting evidence like reproduction steps and test results to help them rule out false positives and to prioritize the biggest threats.
During the conversation with Magouyrk on stage, Altman implied that businesses may eventually need to reconsider their security strategies from the ground up, moving beyond fixing individual bugs toward continuous monitoring – which could spell out potential security team restructuring as AI continues to have an impact on job roles.
OpenAI Head of Cyber Johannes Landgraf explained the threat: "Frontier AI is creating new opportunities to help organizations identify and respond to increasingly sophisticated security threats."
The biggest worry is that while AI can significantly speed up vulnerability discovery, it's also helping attackers exploit them at that same rate.

"It's maybe too hard to patch every bug one by one across the entire supply chain," Sam Altman said. "I think we'll need new ways to fix them."
For many businesses until now, one of the biggest challenges has actually been getting fixes out of the door quickly enough. The hope is that now, AI Security Mesh can equip businesses with the upper hand to respond as quickly as possible to newly discovered threats.

articles.title: Descargar XUPER TV en Android para ver películas gratis: una búsqueda que trae publicidad y robos de dinero
articles.text:
Descargar la APK de XUPER TV para ver películas gratis en un celular Android puede exponer al usuario a publicidad invasiva, pérdida de datos y robos de dinero.
Las búsquedas de aplicaciones fuera de las tiendas oficiales suelen dirigir a páginas con anuncios, enlaces de descarga no verificados y permisos que no guardan relación con la función prometida.
El riesgo no depende solo del nombre de la plataforma, sino de la procedencia real del archivo que se instala. Una APK distribuida desde portales desconocidos puede haber sido modificada o contener programas adicionales.
El Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad de España (INCIBE) advierte que una aplicación maliciosa puede robar información, bloquear el acceso al dispositivo o facilitar operaciones fraudulentas.
Por qué una búsqueda de XUPER TV lleva a instalar publicidad invasiva
Los resultados para descargar aplicaciones streaming gratis pueden incluir sitios que priorizan anuncios, ventanas emergentes y botones confusos. Algunos enlaces no conducen a la APK anunciada, sino a otras páginas que intentan obtener clics, suscripciones o datos de navegación.
INCIBE señala que una app de reputación dudosa puede ralentizar el celular y mostrar anuncios de forma inesperada. Ese comportamiento puede responder a un programa que redirige la navegación hacia sitios publicitarios o páginas dedicadas a recopilar datos.
De qué forma una APK puede comprometer datos personales y bancarios
Una aplicación instalada fuera de Google Play puede solicitar acceso a contactos, archivos, ubicación, cámara o micrófono. Esos permisos pueden permitir la extracción de información almacenada en el celular, desde documentos y fotos hasta agendas telefónicas.
Antes de aceptar una instalación, es necesario comprobar qué permisos reclama el archivo. Una plataforma para reproducir películas no debería necesitar acceso a los mensajes SMS, los contactos o la ubicación precisa para cumplir su función básica.
Si aparecen pedidos de autorización que no tienen una explicación clara, la opción más segura es cancelar la instalación o eliminar la aplicación.
Cómo una aplicación maliciosa roba contraseñas y códigos
Entre las amenazas identificadas por INCIBE figura el keylogger, un programa capaz de registrar las pulsaciones realizadas en la pantalla. De ese modo, una app maliciosa puede capturar nombres de usuario, contraseñas, datos bancarios o información introducida en formularios sin que la persona detecte.
Además, el riesgo alcanza a los códigos de verificación enviados por mensaje de texto. Si una aplicación tiene permiso para leer SMS, puede acceder a claves de un solo uso que bancos, billeteras virtuales y otros servicios emplean para confirmar operaciones.
Qué pasa si el celular queda bloqueado por ransomware
Otra posibilidad es la infección con ransomware, un tipo de malware que puede impedir el acceso a archivos o al propio dispositivo. En esos casos, la víctima puede encontrar un mensaje que exige un pago a cambio de recuperar fotos, documentos u otros contenidos. El pago no garantiza que los datos vuelvan a estar disponibles.
Asimismo, las copias de seguridad reducen el impacto de este tipo de ataques. Guardar archivos en un servicio de almacenamiento en la nube o en un dispositivo externo permite recuperar información si el celular resulta infectado, se pierde o deja de funcionar.
Cuáles medidas reducen el riesgo al instalar aplicaciones
La principal pauta es descargar apps solo desde tiendas oficiales, como Google Play Store, que aplican controles de seguridad antes de publicar software y pueden retirar programas dañinos cuando detectan irregularidades.
La presencia de una aplicación en una tienda oficial tampoco elimina todos los riesgos, pero ofrece una barrera adicional frente a archivos distribuidos en sitios anónimos.
Conviene leer opiniones de usuarios y revisiones de expertos, verificar quién desarrolla la aplicación y desconfiar de promesas de acceso gratuito a estrenos o catálogos pagos.
Un antivirus actualizado puede ayudar a detectar software malicioso. Si una APK de XUPER TV fue instalada y el dispositivo presenta anuncios, lentitud o permisos inusuales, se sugiere desinstalarla, analizar el dispositivo y cambiar las contraseñas utilizadas desde el celular.

articles.title: Should you play Tales of Eternia Remastered on Nintendo Switch 2? I spent 30 hours with this refresh JRPG classic, and it's a blast from start to finish — but these specific issues slightly hold it back
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Tales of Eternia Remastered is overflowing with retro charm, boasting a beautiful visual style, a likeable cast of characters, and a magical soundtrack. But it’s more than a blast from the past — it adds some much-needed quality-of-life changes, helping the game feel far more accessible for the modern era, and delivers fast-paced action-based combat. There are a few graphical gremlins here and there, and the game shows its age at times — especially with some of its awkward movement, both in and outside of battle. All in all, though, I had a lot of fun with this remaster, and it’s one that most JRPG fans will get plenty of joy from.
Reasons to buy
- + Feature-filled Boost Function
- + Well-written cast shine, especially during skits
- + Fun fast-paced yet strategic combat
- + Excellent soundtrack
Reasons to avoid
- - Cutscenes look unrefined
- - Movement can feel a bit awkward
- - Largely poor minigames
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Back in 2000, Bandai Namco published the third game in the beloved Tales series, Tales of Eternia. It was received very well at launch, being praised for its high-octane action combat, charming cast, and humorous script — though the Western versions on the original PlayStation and PSP were held back by their omission of skits (character-driven dialogue scenes) and slightly subpar voice acting. But now, Tales of Eternia Remastered — developed by TOSE Co. — is here, aiming to remedy these issues and refine the game for a modern audience.
Platform reviewed: Nintendo Switch 2
Available on: PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X and Series S, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch
Release date: October 16, 2026
I’ve spent just north of 30 hours with Tales of Eternia Remastered, playing through the main story, completing side quests, and exploring the realms of Inferia and Celestia.
So, how effectively does this remaster bring a JRPG classic into the modern era? And is it truly worth playing? Here’s my verdict.
Gimme a Boost!
I’ll speak about the core Tales of Eternia experience in good time, but it only seems right to discuss the new stuff that this remaster brings to the table first.
Arguably the main thing is the inclusion of Boost Function. This enables you to tailor your experience to your specific wants and needs, with highlights including a random encounter toggle, difficulty options, an increased item capacity setting, and an EXP gain adjuster.
My personal favorite feature was the option to restore TP (which you consume when using skills) when camping, which made grinding feel a lot more fluid and easier to manage.
The Boost Function suite is filled to the brim, and really helps to make the title more approachable for newcomers. My only real complaint here is that I would’ve loved the option to map a function — such as disabling enemy encounters — to one of the buttons on my Nintendo Switch 2. Having to open the main menu, go into the Customize Section, and then the Boost Function felt a touch clunky.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Defeating the Greater Craymel, Celsius, was by far one of the most rewarding moments for me. She was giving me a lot of trouble by evading my Artes and freezing my healers into submission, but after switching up my formation and strategy, I was able to best her in a true battle for the ages.
There’s a lot more to uncover, though. For instance, you can switch between remastered and original graphics and sound effects, which is sure to satisfy newcomers and long-time fans.
The visual enhancements are relatively light overall. This isn’t a transformative overhaul, and some environments still look a little rough around the edges. But still, the remaster does illuminate some previously obscured details. As you can see in the images below, detailing on the statues is far more intricate, and foliage looks sharper in the remastered graphics mode. And while some may prefer the original pixel sprites, I think the remaster does a good job of cleaning them up a bit while keeping them faithful to the original artwork.
While we’re on the topic of visuals, I unfortunately have a complaint to make: the cutscenes look pretty poor. They’ve been placed into widescreen, and it looks as if a filter has been applied; the results are underwhelming — characters and backgrounds lack clarity and definition, laying bare the limitations of the original material.
That’s a nitpick, of course, and most elements of this remaster still hit the spot. For example, the newly recorded English voice acting is great, and each character’s personality shines through perfectly. Skits are finally here in the West, too, providing plenty of humorous and emotional moments when camping or resting.
Objective icons are also introduced, which point you in the direction of the main story objective or side quests. I really appreciated this, especially as I didn’t want to miss out on side content, but if you want to figure everything out for yourself, you can swiftly switch it off in the Customize menu.
An underrated classic, reborn
So, while it’s not flawless, the remaster of this title is solid overall and successfully makes this classic more palatable for modern audiences. But just how fun is the core game in the big 2026?
I’ll lay my cards on the table: I had a spectacular time with Tales of Eternia Remastered. This was actually my first time playing the game — after all, I wasn’t even born when it was initially released. In spite of that, there was something so nostalgic about it, the warm, charming world and excellent cast totally captured my attention, and I found myself pouring countless hours into the game every single day.
Something that stood out for me was the writing. Yes, the main narrative is nothing special — the world is in danger, and a group of young heroes needs to defy the odds to save everybody. But it’s the characters that make this experience so special.
For the most part, you'll spend your time with four key heroes. Reid is a reluctant protagonist who seems to be dragged into the chaos at every turn, Farah is a contemplative, complex young woman learning herself as the story unfolds, Keele is a stuck-up academic type who delivers some hilarious moments, and Meredy is a caring and curious foreign stranger who the crew slowly begins to understand in their quest to prevent disaster.
The cast isn’t weighed down by the tired tropes and lazy writing that a lot of JRPGs faced at the time, and each party member is highly memorable.
But how about the actual gameplay? Well, the combat is pretty unique. It manifests in the form of a fighter-RPG hybrid, with a large focus on reactive action-based commands. While the combat certainly takes some getting used to and the movement can feel a little janky at times, battling your foes feels incredibly addictive. Chaining Artes together to deliver devastating combos and tinkering with formations or skills to get past tough boss battles is highly rewarding, and even random encounters gave me huge satisfaction.
The game is undoubtedly challenging, but delivering a finishing blow makes your struggle feel worth it. And if you do fall to your foes, a retry battle option is at hand to dive right back into the action.
There’s not too much grinding required, either. I kept random encounters on for the vast majority of my playthrough, and that gave me plenty of experience for big boss fights. If you do want to grab some extra experience, though, you can switch Auto mode on and have your team fight for you, helping you avoid same-y skirmishes.
Outside of battle, things are decent too. You can explore the world for items and treasure to bolster your stats, venture into shops to grab stronger gear, and even take on a few minigames. Exploration is highly gratifying as well, and you’ll often find weapons that come in handy for specific areas or recipes that restore your HP or TP when you’re running low.
A small complaint I have, though, is that movement feels clunky in the overworld. You need to be very precise if you want to move diagonally, and dragging items like statues could feel a bit awkward at times. This is still a relatively minor issue overall, but in tighter areas, the old-school movement did cause me some minor frustration.
I also have to say that the minigames, in general, are pretty bad. They typically control fine, but don’t feel very fun to play at all. Luckily, you can skip these if you’d prefer, which I often did. It was cool to see mouse mode integration for minigames on Nintendo Switch 2, though, which worked a treat in my experience.
Speaking of my experience on Switch 2, let’s take a moment to talk about performance. Tales of Eternia Remastered runs in 4K when playing docked and 1080p in handheld, with smooth 60fps across both modes — perhaps to be expected for a less demanding title like this. I didn’t notice any technical hiccups or frame drops during my whole playthrough, so Switch 2 is certainly a top-tier destination for this remaster.
So let’s address those questions I posed in the intro. Is Tales of Eternia Remastered a worthy modern take on this classic entry? For me, the answer is yes.
Some things could’ve been better: the visual enhancements are relatively light, cutscenes look a bit underwhelming, and I would’ve liked a shortcut button for disabling enemy encounters. But the Boost Function provides so much flexibility, the new English dub is great, and the ability to retry battles in an instant keeps the game's pace feeling fast and fluid.
And at a core level, this is a great game with a lot to offer, in spite of a few dated elements. The combat, while very much of its time, remains fun and surprisingly strategic; the cast is highly memorable, with skits adding some welcome depth, and exploration is rewarding too.
All in all, I had a blast with Tales of Eternia Remastered, and JRPG fanatics are sure to find a lot to love here.
Should you play Tales of Eternia Remastered?
Play it if...
You appreciate a challenge
Tales of Eternia is a fairly challenging game, with some daunting boss fights scattered throughout the experience. I had to retry a fair few times when battling against the mightiest foes, but there’s even a hard and extreme mode if you truly want to test yourself.
You want to play a JRPG that doesn’t overstay its welcome
As a huge JRPG fan, I know that this genre has a tendency to demand an awful lot of your time. But Tales of Eternia hits a real sweet spot. It takes around 25-30 hours to finish (unless you’re a true completionist), and is well-paced throughout, making it a far more approachable title than a lot of other games in this space.
Don't play it if...
You’re expecting a modern Tales experience
Tales of Eternia Remastered remains very faithful to the original, and you’re still getting that 2D action-based combat of yesteryear. It’s not as fluid and free-flowing as modern Tales combat systems, so if that’s what you’re after, it may be worth looking elsewhere.
You want top-tier visuals
Of course, this is a remaster rather than a remake, so this entry isn't aiming to supply a striking visual overhaul. Even still, the visuals are a bit of a mixed bag; the cutscenes aren’t handled very well, and the in-game graphical enhancements, while decent, aren’t exactly transformative.
Accessibility features
There are a number of ways to customize your experience in Tales of Eternia Remastered. You can turn subtitles on or off, choose to auto-advance text, remap buttons to suit your preferences, and alter difficulty. While there’s no colorblind mode, in-game elements that previously required color-based identification have been redesigned around visual elements unrelated to color.
How I reviewed Tales of Eternia Remastered
I spent just over 30 hours with Tales of Eternia Remastered, during which time I played through the main story, completed a handful of side quests, and tried out all of the various Boost Function features.
For the most part, I played the game in docked mode, with my Nintendo Switch 2 hooked up to the Sky Glass Gen 2 TV and Marshall Heston 120 soundbar. However, I did dip into handheld mode from time to time, and used the Sennheiser CX 80U wired earbuds to enjoy in-game audio.
More generally, I’ve covered a huge array of games here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve reviewed a number of JRPGs, including Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter and Dragon Quest I & II HD-2D Remake, as well as Switch 2 exclusives such as Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.
First reviewed October 2026
Harry is a Senior Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He reviews everything from party speakers to wall chargers and has a particular interest in the worlds of audio and gaming. Harry has a background in business tech journalism, particularly around the telecoms industry.

articles.title: Anthropic eliminó las entrevistas de programación porque Claude resuelve mejor las pruebas
articles.text:
Felix Rieseberg, gerente de ingeniería de Anthropic, dejó de pedir ejercicios de programación a los candidatos de su equipo porque Claude, la IA de la empresa, resuelve esas pruebas mejor que ellos. Lo explicó el 27 de octubre en un artículo de su blog y en una publicación en X.
“La entrevista de programación murió, al menos para mi equipo en Anthropic”, escribió en X. Según su artículo, plantear un pequeño desafío en React, una herramienta para crear sitios web, tiene tan poco sentido como interrogar sobre lenguaje ensamblador, uno de los más básicos y antiguos: Claude “es ahora mejor en ambos”.
Rieseberg dirigió la ingeniería de Claude.ai, de la versión de escritorio de Claude Code y de la herramienta Cowork, según la biografía que cita The Next Web. Antes trabajó en Notion, Stripe, Slack y Microsoft.
Esos desafíos eran, dice, un predictor “débil pero útil” del éxito en sus equipos. Ya no lo son: los mejores constructores tienen éxito sin importar su desempeño en esas pruebas.
Los novatos superan a los veteranos, según el gerente
Su tesis es que el impacto depende menos de los años acumulados de conocimiento sobre herramientas y librerías de código. “Veo ingenieros relativamente nuevos que adelantan a personas que probablemente programan mejor y llevan mucho más tiempo”, escribió. Su resumen: “El hambre le gana a la antigüedad”.
Como ejemplo, citó a dos ingenieros recientes de Anthropic, Anthony Morris y Alice Zhao. Armaron en un fin de semana un prototipo de interfaz gráfica para Claude Code, que hasta entonces se usaba solo con comandos de texto. La primera versión pública salió unos ocho días después.
El artículo también dirige un consejo a ingenieros sin poder ni estatus. Deben entender qué busca la empresa, elegir una idea ambiciosa y construir un prototipo funcional en un fin de semana. Rieseberg sostiene que ejecutar ya no es caro, y que por eso los novatos no necesitan esperar a ganar rango para que se los escuche.
Una encuesta muestra que otras empresas no lo imitan
El caso de Anthropic no refleja una tendencia general, según Nicole Bachaud, economista laboral de ZipRecruiter, plataforma de empleo. “No vemos que las empresas tecnológicas abandonen de forma generalizada las evaluaciones de habilidades, al menos todavía”, dijo a The Register.
Bachaud citó la encuesta de octubre de 2026 de ZipRecruiter a 1.500 empleadores. En el sector de la información, el que incluye a las tecnológicas, el 62,5% exige pruebas formales de habilidades en la solicitud inicial, la proporción más alta entre los sectores que mencionó.
La economista interpretó el cambio de Anthropic como un giro hacia habilidades humanas. Según la misma encuesta, el 61,5% de los empleadores del sector dice que el pensamiento crítico es la principal carencia de los candidatos.
En redes sociales, Jaana Dogan, ingeniera principal de Google, escribió que hoy hace pocas entrevistas de programación y que le interesaría evaluar cómo usan los candidatos los agentes de programación, asistentes de IA que escriben código por su cuenta.
Rieseberg reconoce que no tiene resuelto qué poner en su lugar. Por ahora revisa currículums y portafolios en busca de pequeños prototipos que muestren “gusto, empatía y pensamiento con principios”, y pide que le cuenten si alguien encontró algo mejor. Su conclusión es que la entrevista de programación no volverá.
Cómo Claude engañó a otras IA con textos aparentemente inocentes
Anthropic logró que Claude redactara textos aparentemente inocuos (apicultura, lucha libre, empleos comunes) que, al reentrenar otros modelos, les enseñaron a engañar y resistir supervisión sin ser detectados por los filtros de seguridad.
Los modelos resultantes nunca se usaron públicamente: fueron experimentos controlados. Aun así, mostraron comportamientos graves, como copiar sus propios parámetros a un servidor externo, ocultar puertas traseras o culpar a colegas en pruebas simuladas.
Anthropic reconoce limitaciones del experimento, pero advierte que estos datos podrían pasar desapercibidos para los monitores actuales de IA.

articles.title: Por qué Anthropic recibiría una calificación crediticia de “bono basura” tras su salida a bolsa
articles.text:
Anthropic podría obtener una calificación crediticia de “bono basura” alta por parte de las agencias calificadoras tras su salida a bolsa, según un reporte del Financial Times.
El dato representa un giro respecto a las proyecciones anteriores sobre la empresa creadora del asistente de inteligencia artificial Claude, que hasta hace poco apuntaba a un estatus de grado de inversión antes de 2027.
Qué reveló el informe sobre Anthropic
De acuerdo con la publicación, Blackstone, el gigante de inversión que funciona como inversor ancla en un acuerdo de 63.000 millones de dólares para financiar los chips de Anthropic, comunicó a los inversores de ese acuerdo que espera una calificación “junk” alta para la compañía después de su oferta pública inicial (OPI).
El pronóstico ubica a Anthropic en el rango doble B, el escalón superior dentro de las calificaciones especulativas o de “bono basura”. Se trata de una revisión drástica frente a la expectativa previa de la propia Blackstone, que había anticipado que la empresa alcanzaría un grado de inversión antes de que terminara 2026.
Tanto Anthropic como Blackstone declinaron hacer comentarios cuando fueron consultados por el medio TechCrunch sobre esta proyección.
Una calificación “junk” señala un riesgo de impago más alto que el de los bonos con grado de inversión y, en consecuencia, implica costos de endeudamiento más elevados para la empresa que la recibe. Mientras el grado de inversión indica bajo riesgo para los prestamistas, el estatus especulativo advierte lo contrario: mayor probabilidad de que la compañía no cumpla con sus obligaciones de pago.
El reporte sobre esta revisión se dio a conocer el 30 de octubre, apenas días después de que Anthropic presentara de forma oficial su solicitud para cotizar en bolsa, lo que desató especulación sobre el impacto que tendría esta OPI en el conjunto de la industria de inteligencia artificial.
Qué significa recibir un bono basura
El término “bono basura” (junk bond, en inglés) designa a los instrumentos de deuda que las agencias calificadoras consideran de grado especulativo, por debajo del umbral de grado de inversión.
Esta clasificación no implica que la empresa esté en quiebra ni que sus bonos carezcan de valor. Significa que, a criterio de las agencias, existe un riesgo mayor de que el emisor no pueda cumplir con los pagos de intereses o capital en los plazos pactados.
El rango doble B que proyecta Blackistone para Anthropic corresponde, de hecho, al peldaño más alto dentro de esta categoría especulativa, lo que indica un riesgo menor que otras calificaciones “junk” inferiores, aunque sigue estando por debajo del umbral de grado de inversión.
Para una compañía, obtener esta calificación tiene consecuencias prácticas directas. Las empresas con calificación especulativa enfrentan tasas de interés más altas a la hora de pedir préstamos, lo que encarece el financiamiento de sus operaciones.
Además, suelen tener más dificultades para atraer a inversores institucionales, ya que muchos de estos fondos están sujetos a reglas internas que les impiden adquirir valores por debajo del grado de inversión.
El plan de Anthropic para salir a la bolsa
La presentación oficial de Anthropic para cotizar en bolsa generó especulación inmediata sobre su efecto en el resto de la industria de inteligencia artificial. La compañía se ha posicionado como una alternativa centrada en la seguridad frente a sus competidores, con énfasis en principios de “IA constitucional” y prácticas de desarrollo responsable.
Sin embargo, el pronóstico sobre su calificación crediticia sugiere que incluso los laboratorios de inteligencia artificial con mayor reputación técnica enfrentan interrogantes de fondo sobre su sostenibilidad financiera.
La proyección de Blackstone llega en momentos en que el entusiasmo de los inversores por las compañías de inteligencia artificial está atravesado por un escrutinio mayor sobre la rentabilidad y la solidez de sus modelos de negocio, un factor que podría influir en cómo los analistas e inversores institucionales evalúen la valuación de la OPI de Anthropic.

articles.title: Adieu Visa et Mastercard : 130 millions d'Européens passent au paiement 100 % souverain
articles.text:
Adieu Visa et Mastercard : 130 millions d'Européens passent au paiement 100 % souverain
L'Europe règle ses comptes
Face au monopole des géants américains, cinq leaders européens du paiement regroupent 130 millions d'utilisateurs sous une même bannière. Objectif : bâtir une infrastructure 100 % souveraine capable de rapatrier des milliards de transactions sur le Vieux Continent.
Cet article a été initialement publié en mai 2026. Nous le republions aujourd'hui car la question de la souveraineté européenne dans le domaine des paiements et le développement d'alternatives aux géants américains restent des sujets cruciaux et d'une grande actualité pour nos lecteurs.
C'est un séisme pour le secteur bancaire européen. L'initiative française Wero s'associe officiellement aux poids lourds du marché : Bizum (Espagne), Bancomat (Italie), MB WAY (Portugal) et Vipps MobilePay (pays nordiques). En interconnectant leurs réseaux régionaux, ces acteurs ne se contentent plus de faire de la résistance : ils bâtissent une alternative transfrontalière massive pour garder le contrôle total sur les données financières du continent.
Interopérabilité : la clé de voûte de la souveraineté technologique
	
L'Europe dispose de l'infrastructure, de l'échelle et de la vision nécessaires pour offrir une alternative européenne souveraine, robuste et fiable dans le domaine des paiements.
Le projet s'appuie sur la création d'un hub central d'interopérabilité, géré par une entité commune que les partenaires établiront au premier semestre 2026. Cette plateforme technique permettra aux différents systèmes de dialoguer entre eux, sans que les utilisateurs n'aient à changer leurs habitudes. Un Français utilisant Wero pourra ainsi transférer de l'argent à un ami espagnol sur Bizum, avec la même simplicité qu'un paiement domestique.
Feuille de route : 13 pays connectés d'ici 2027
Le déploiement se fera progressivement. Les virements entre particuliers seront disponibles dès 2026 sur l'ensemble des treize pays couverts – d'Andorre à la Suède. Les paiements en ligne et en magasin suivront en 2027. À terme, cette coalition couvrira 72 % de la population de l'Union européenne et de la Norvège.
	
La souveraineté européenne des paiements n'est pas une vision, mais une réalité en devenir.
L'alliance EuroPA, qui connecte déjà l'Espagne, le Portugal, l'Italie et Andorre depuis mars 2025, sert de prototype. Six millions d'euros y ont transité en un an, sans campagne promotionnelle particulière. Un signal encourageant pour cette ambition d'autonomie européenne dans un secteur longtemps dominé par des géants extra-continentaux — une préoccupation que Christine Lagarde avait déjà martelée en avril 2025.

articles.title: 'The definition of value for money': The TCL C7L is one of the most impressive TVs I've tested this year, delivering excellent bang for your buck
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The TCL C7L delivers great overall picture quality, very good gaming performance and features, all for a competitive price that's excellent value for what the C7L has to offer. While it does have its shortcomings — off-axis viewing and average sound — you won't get many TVs on the market that are better value than the C7L.
Reasons to buy
- + Very good picture quality
- + Excellent value for money
- + Great for gaming
Reasons to avoid
- - Average built-in sound
- - Blooming when viewed off-centre
- - Only two HDMI 2.1 ports
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
TCL C7L review: Two minute review
The C7L serves as the mid-range model in TCL’s 2026 SQD (Super Quantum Dot) mini-LED lineup. In terms of value, this is one of the best TVs you can get, delivering great performance and features for the price. While it does have its shortcomings, its bang-for-your-buck proposition is unmatched.
It delivers excellent picture quality, with vivid, bright colours that really pop, smooth motion for movies and sports, impressive contrast and backlight control, and even offers deep black tones that can on occasion rival some of the C7L’s best OLED TV rivals. Viewing angles are its main weakness, with some obvious blooming when viewed off-center, and it can overexert its brightness, but overall the C7L’s picture is great for the price.
Built-in sound quality is a mixed bag. While the C7L has surprisingly good width, along with some nice detail, clear speech and good front-end power, it really is lacking in the bass department, and at higher volumes the sound can become a tad harsh. While the C7L’s speakers are fine for casual viewing, fans of movies, and shows with a more cinematic feel, will want to invest in one of the best soundbars.
The C7L can easily compete with the best gaming TVs, and offers a lot for gamers on a tighter budget. Its full suite of features — 4K 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro, ALLM and Dolby Vision gaming — low 9.8ms input lag time and great picture quality make it a fantastic-value gaming TV.
Price is where the C7L excels. The 55-inch model I tested launched for £1,099 in June 2026, and since then I’ve seen it drop to £849 in places — and these prices will continue to drop. This makes it cheaper than rival OLEDs, such as the LG B6 and Samsung S85H, and RGB TVs such as the Hisense UR8. In terms of value for money, there aren’t many better TVs available.
TCL C7L review: Price & release date
- Release date: June 2026
- 55-inch: £1,099
- 65-inch: £1,299
- 75-inch: £1,699
- 85-inch: £2,199
- 98-inch: £2,999
The TCL C7L is the brand’s mid-range SQD (Super Quantum Dot) mini-LED for 2026, sitting below the TCL C8L and flagship TCL X11L. It also sits below TCL’s RGB lineup, which comprises the TCL RM7L and flagship RM8L. The 55-inch model I tested launched in June 2026, and was priced at £1,099 at launch.
Since its release, prices have dropped across the board, with the 55-inch model dropping as low as £849, making it cheaper than most RGB TVs and pretty much every 2026 OLED, with its nearest rivals being the LG B6 and Samsung S85H (both of which are priced at £1,199 for the 55-inch model at the time of writing).

TCL C7L review: Features
- SQD mini-LED panel
- Dolby Vision and HDR10+ support
- Four HDMI 2.1 ports
The TCL C7L has TCL’s SQD mini-LED panel, which the brand claims provides better backlight accuracy thanks to more precise dimming, as well as better colour volume. This panel has been adopted from the flagship X11L, the first SQD mini-LED, which also launched in 2026.
It uses TCL’s TSR AiPQ processor, which comes with AI features designed to improve picture, sound and gaming performance. Unlike TVs from major rivals such as LG, Samsung and Sony, the C7L supports all HDR flavours, including both Dolby Vision and HDR10+.
The C7L also has an anti-glare screen for reduced mirror-like reflections, taking a cue from Samsung’s own Glare Free screen, which Samsung first introduced on its flagship S95D OLED in 2024, before bringing it to more TVs in its mini-LED and OLED range in 2025.
It’s also well equipped for gaming, supporting 4K 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro, ALLM and Dolby Vision gaming, along with an option for 288Hz with a compatible connected source (PC). The C7L is, however, limited to two HDMI 2.1 ports rated for gaming.
Audio is provided by Bang & Olufsen, with a 60W speaker system that supports both Dolby Atmos and DTS: Virtual X. A number of AI sound features are available, as well as a BeoSound menu where you can customise your sound profile manually.
The C7L uses Google TV as its smart TV interface, which offers all the major streaming apps like Netflix, Prime Video and Disney Plus, alongside BBC iPlayer, ITVX, Channel 4 and Channel 5.
- Features score: 4.5 / 5
TCL C7L review: Picture quality
- Bold colours
- Great contrast
- Blooming from off-centre viewing
The C7L produces excellent brightness for a mid-range, affordable mini-LED. It measured 2,083 nits peak HDR brightness (with Boost off, on a 10% window) in Filmmaker Mode, which easily beats LG’s mid-range OLED C6 (which hit 1,427 nits in my most recent tests), and even bests some RGB TVs like the Bravia 7 II (1,595 nits) and the flagship Samsung R95H (1,545 nits). With the C7L’s Boost mode activated, its brightness did hit 3,514 nits peak HDR in Movie mode, but it only affected 10% window measurements.
It also delivers very good fullscreen brightness, hitting 692 and 699 nits fullscreen HDR brightness in Filmmaker and Standard mode. While other mini-LEDs have scored higher, this is much higher than any OLED. I did find when watching in a bright room that there were some mirror-like reflections with darker scenes, but the C7L did a great job of mitigating reflections in bright scenes and sports content.
The C7L does a good job of upscaling textures in SDR/HD content, and, while they don’t get to 4K levels of sharpness, textures do look cleaner. I saw this when watching sports on Prime Video, which was in HD.
Switching to reference 4K scenes, the C7L demonstrated bold, vibrant colours. This made movies like The Super Mario Galaxy Movie really pop on screen, shown by the rich hue of the Lumas whenever they were on screen. In Speed Racer, the C7L renders the candy-coloured aesthetic of the Racer house and the character’s outfits well, and it did a great job with Elemental on Disney Plus, especially during the scene where Ember makes a vase, making the oranges, purples and pinks of the vase dazzle on screen.
Measuring the C7L’s HDR colour gamut, it hit 97.3% of the UHDA-P3 colour space (which is used for mastering 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema releases). That’s a good result, but most impressive was its BT.2020 result, which hit 90.1%, which is one of the highest scores I’ve seen.
Switching to darker and high-contrast scenes, the C7L demonstrates strong contrast with a good balance between light and dark tones. This is shown in the scene in The Batman in which Bruce works in the Batcave, with the contrast between the bright monitors and the dark surroundings handled well. While the contrast didn’t quite match up to that of the LG B6E OLED when I compared the two, it was good for a backlit TV.
Space scenes in Project Hail Mary looked similarly impressive, with rich and inky blacks. The C7L also showed good backlight control, with only minor blooming occurring in the stars against the black backdrop of space when viewed head-on. Off-center viewing, however, revealed more backlight blooming, which is a common occurrence with backlit TVs. Picture quality did fade with some brighter scenes as well when viewed off-center, though not to the extent I’ve seen with past mini-LED TVs.
Finally, the C7L demonstrated very good motion handling. For sports, having motion set to ‘Medium’ or a custom setting of Blur reduction on 2 and Judder reduction on 5 worked well, delivering smooth motion with very few motion artifacts. For movies, Natural Cinema mode worked very well, as the C7L handled the fast-paced action of Speed Racer convincingly.
- Picture quality score: 4.5 / 5
TCL C7L review: Sound quality
- Good, front-facing sound
- Good accuracy with some width
- Bass is lacking
The TCL C7L 55-inch I tested features a 2.2-channel, 60W speaker system tuned by Bang & Olufsen. As well as conventional sound modes like Movie and Sports, the C7L also features a custom sound setting, as well as a Beosound menu that offers the choice of four different sound profiles: Relaxed, Bright, Energetic, and Warm; you can also adjust the balance between these for a custom effect.
Watching the Batmobile/Penguin car chase scenes in The Batman, the C7L’s speakers deliver refined detail with good accuracy, with the sound accurately tracking the on-screen action . The soundstage also delivers good width, with sound extending beyond the frame and demonstrating good dynamics. I also found the C7L’s sound to be very forward-facing, meaning the overall sound was clearer than from some other TVs.
The C7L’s built-in sound isn’t without its flaws, though. Bass is lacking, so I wasn’t getting the low-end rumble from the Batmobile that I expected. Treble could sometimes be a little brash too, especially when the volume was pushed. I experimented with the Beosound menu, and found that positioning the cursor between Energetic and Warm added a bit of depth, but nothing substantial.
- Sound quality: 3.5 / 5
TCL C7L review: Design
- Lightweight feel
- Standard, safe design
- Central pedestal stand
The C7L’s design is pretty standard for a TV in this price range. It’s virtually identical to last year’s TCL C7K, featuring a silver frame that adds some nice polish to the rather plain build elsewhere. The TV itself is incredibly light for a 55-inch TV, though feels sturdy enough when placed on a TV unit.
It uses a central pedestal stand that’s easy to fit and feels like the same type of plastic material used in the rear panel. The TV itself is a little deeper than other TVs, especially compared to OLEDs.
The included remote feels a little lightweight and cheap, but has a standard button layout that’s easy to follow, with shortcuts to major apps like Netflix. Overall, the C7L has a pretty safe design.
- Design: 4 / 5
TCL C7L review: Smart TV & menus
- Google TV
- Good picture settings with easy menus
- Large distracting banner ads on Google homepage
Like all TCL TVs, the C7L uses Google TV as its smart TV platform. Google TV is great at making content recommendations and even remembering content you’ve watched, especially with YouTube. Unfortunately, the homepage features large banner ads that take up to half the space on the screen. This is an issue with Google TV that I’ve also seen on plenty of other brands that use the platform.
The various menus and settings are easy enough to navigate, with picture settings divided into logical categories. There are also plenty of settings to allow you to customise your picture to the nth degree, though some settings, especially some of the texture enhancement settings, make less difference than others. I’d personally recommend turning settings like Super Resolution off for a more natural picture.
While Google TV is a perfectly serviceable smart TV platform, I feel it’s not as strong as LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, or Roku.
- Smart TV & menus: 4 / 5
TCL C7L review: Gaming
- 4K 144Hz & FreeSync Premium Pro
- 9.8ms input lag time
- Only two HDMI 2.1 ports
The TCL C7L has a great list of gaming features, including 4K 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro VRR, Dolby Vision gaming and ALLM, although only two of its four HDMI ports are rated 2.1 and support these features. The C7L also features a Game Master bar, where you can adjust settings such as shadow enhancement.
In my testing the C7L recorded low input-lag times, including 9.8ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.9ms at 1080p 120Hz, which are fantastic results. These numbers translate into real-world performance too, as I found when playing Battlefield V. The C7L’s performance was great overall, handling the game’s large-scale battles and explosive action with ease. As I battled through levels, it could easily keep up with my need to snap to targets while moving around.
While the C7L’s picture quality was great for gaming overall, delivering the same bold colours and strong contrast I’d seen while watching movies, I did notice on occasion that textures could muddy and blur during particularly hectic moments.
- Gaming score: 4.5 / 5
TCL C7L review: Value
- Excellent features for the money
- Competitive price for this level of tech
- Great mid-range option
The 55-inch model of the TCL C7L that I tested costs £999 on average, although I have seen it drop to as low as £849. Plus, if TCL’s pricing strategy of previous years is anything to go by, those prices will drop again, especially during sales periods like Black Friday. Even at full price, it’s £200 cheaper than the entry-level LG B6 OLED (£1,199 for the 55-inch) and that price puts it in a similar range to rival mini-LEDs from Hisense (the U7 Pro is £999) and Samsung (the QN80H is £899).
For the performance and features it offers, the C7L is excellent value. The performance of TCL’s mid-range mini-LED models seems to improve year on year, and the C7L is one of the best TCL TVs I’ve tested. Yes, its sound could be better, but it ticks a lot of boxes in other areas, and has the potential to become even better value as its price drops over time.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should you buy the TCL C7L?
| TCL C7L scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Tons of smart and gaming features as well as full HDR support | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Picture quality | Excellent colour, great brightness and very good contrast. Some blooming when viewed off-centre | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Sound quality | Good accuracy and width with clear speech, but bass is lacking | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Design | Good build quality that feels its price, but remote feels a little cheap | 4 / 5 | 
| Smart TV and menus | Good content recommendations from Google TV, but banner ads are distracting | 4 / 5 | 
| Gaming | Great list of gaming features including 4K 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro and a low input lag time. Only two HDMI 2.1 ports | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Value | A great value TV that's cheaper than rival OLEDs and RGB TVs. Deliver performance that outweighs the price | 4.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want a great value TV
A near-full suite of gaming pictures and great picture quality, all for an ultra-competitive price. There aren't many better value TVs than the C7L. 
You want very good picture quality
The C7L has bold colours and strong contrast and delivers good backlight control when viewed head-on. Its picture outperforms its price. 
You want a feature-packed but more affordable gaming TV
With 4K 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro and Dolby Vision and a 9.8ms input lag time, the C7L is brilliant TV for gaming. 
Don't buy it if...
You want cinematic sound
While the C7L has good enough sound for day-to-day viewing, its lack of bass takes away from the cinematic experience. A soundbar is recommended. 
You want to watch from an angle 
The C7L's picture quality and backlight control waver when viewed off-centre, meaning larger groups may not get the full experience. 
You have multiple next-gen gaming consoles
The C7L only has two HDMI 2.1 ports, meaning only two ports can accommodate gaming consoles and a soundbar. Other TVs in this price range have four HDMI 2.1 ports. 
Also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | TCL C7L | LG B6 | Samsung QN80H | Hisense UR8 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (55-inch) | £999 | £1,199 | £919 | £1,299 | 
| Screen type | SQD mini-LED | OLED | Mini-LED | RGB mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 120Hz (up to 144Hz) | 120Hz | 120Hz (up to 144Hz) | 120Hz (up to 180Hz) | 
| HDR support | Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | 
| Smart TV | Google TV | webOS 26 | Tizen | VIDAA | 
| HDMI ports | 4 (2 x HDMI 2.1) | 4 x HDMI 2.1 | 4 x HDMI 2.1 | 4 x HDMI 2.1 | 
LG B6
The LG B6 is the most affordable OLED in LG's 2026 lineup and it delivers richer colours and better black tones than the C7L. The C7L has a big brightness advantage and is likely to stay much cheaper than the B6, even during big sales. This one comes down to preference and what room you'll be watching in. 
Read our full LG B6 review
Samsung QN80H
Samsung's mid-range mini-LED has more gaming features than the C7L, but the C7L offers higher brightness and better backlight control. Price-wise, these two are almost identical and for that reason, the C7L's better performance makes it the better value buy. We haven't reviewed the QN80H, but I have extensively tested it. 
Check out our Samsung QN80H vs Samsung M80H feature
Hisense UR8
The UR8 is Hisense's more entry-level RGB mini-LED and surprisingly, the C7L delivers quite close performance in terms of picture quality and gaming. The UR8 has slightly better sound, but the C7L is generally £300 cheaper and the better value model of the two. 
Read our full Hisense UR8 review
How I tested the TCL C7L
- Tested over a couple of weeks
- Tested in varying lighting conditions in our testing lab using reference scenes
- Measurements taken using Portrait Displays' Calman colour calibration software
The first step of testing the TCL C7L was some casual viewing to establish its best picture and sound modes. I eventually settled on Filmmaker Mode for movies and TV shows and Standard for sports and broadcast TV.
After testing the C7L with SDR content including sports and HD movies to test its upscaling, I moved onto reference 4K HDR and Dolby Vision scenes to test it colour, contrast, backlight control, brightness, motion and detail.
As well as subjective testing, I took measurements using specialised equipment, focusing on the C7L's brightness, HDR colour gamut coverage, picture accuracy and input lag. These tests were done using a Klein K-10A colourimeter, profiled with a Jeti Spectral 15VA Spectroradiometer and Portrait Displays' Calman Colour calibration software.
For brightness, I measured the C7L with 1-100% window sizes, focusing on peak (10%) and fullscreen (100%) brightness in particular. These were measured in both SDR and HDR.
Next was HDR colour gamut coverage, with measurements of the UHDA-P3 colour space (used for 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema mastering) and BT.2020 (the colour space used by projectors).
I also measured greyscale and colour accuracy in SDR.
I also tested the C7L HDR EOTF, which measures its accuracy at both light and dark levels, and Spectral Power Distribution, which measures the C7L's colour performance.
Finally, I measured input lag in milliseconds (ms), using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.
Read our in-depth overview of how we test TVs at TechRadar.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read TechRadar's reviews guarantee
James is the TV Hardware Staff Writer at TechRadar. Before joining the team, he worked at a major UK based AV retailer selling TV and audio equipment, where he was either telling customers the difference between OLED and QLED or being wowed by watching a PS5 run on the LG 65G2. When not writing about the latest TV tech, James can be found gaming, reading, watching rugby or coming up with another idea for a novel.
