articles.title: Hackers Steal About $2.7 Million From Polymarket Traders via Hijacked DebugBear Script
articles.text:
Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company.
Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour.
The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors.
Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script.
DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking.
Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's.
How the Script Took the Money
The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys.
Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to.
Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions.
It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out.
In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session.
The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets.
At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions.
The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows.
Polymarket's Response and Refunds
Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused.
The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement.
By October 30, 689 of the 726 affected wallets had been refunded in full, and the remaining 37 were being paid as they were checked. Polymarket is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken. In all, it is returning $3.9 million to traders.
Traders do not need to file a claim. Polymarket's status page links a form for anyone who thinks their amount is wrong or that they should have received a payment.
What Sites and Traders Can Do
DebugBear has told customers of its RUM product to remove its embed code from their websites. The address that served the malicious file, cdn.debugbear[.]com, had no DNS record when The Hacker News checked on November 1.
Polymarket said it is putting third-party scripts back in place with extra checks, such as a stronger Content Security Policy (CSP), pinned versions, and sandboxing.
Hudson Rock's advice for sites that load outside scripts:
- Keep unneeded third-party code off pages where users trade or sign.
- Where a file can be pinned, use Subresource Integrity (SRI), which lets the browser reject the file if its contents change. A security policy that simply allows a trusted CDN does not check the files that CDN serves.
- Check what code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do.
Hudson Rock's advice for traders is to reject any signing request they did not expect.

articles.title: Finnland gegen Google: KI-Pläne und illegale Rodungen sorgen für Spannungen
articles.text:
„Ich will sie hier nicht“: Googles KI-Pläne sorgen in Finnland für Kritik
Vor einigen Monaten standen bei Muhos im Norden Finnlands auf einer rund 330 Hektar großen Fläche noch mehrere hunderttausende Bäume – von dem Wald ist heute nichts mehr übrig. „Es bleibt nur noch eine riesige Schlammfläche zurück, durchzogen von Spurrillen der Maschinen, Pfützen und Erdhaufen, Wurzeln und Ästen“, heißt es in einer Recherche des Guardians. Anwohner:innen von Muhos berichten dem Guardian außerdem, dass braunes Wasser vom Gelände in einen Bach sickert. Wenige hundert Meter weiter mündet der Bach in den Fluss Oulujoki.
Google ließ diese Fläche bei Muhos für ein geplantes Rechenzentrum roden. Auch der Oberboden – also die oberste, humusreiche und nährstoffhaltige Erdschicht – wurde abgetragen. Die erforderlichen Umweltverträglichkeitsprüfungen durch die finnische Aufsichtsbehörde waren zu diesem Zeitpunkt allerdings nicht abgeschlossen. Daraufhin ordnete die Behörde den vorläufigen Stopp der Arbeiten in Muhos sowie an einem weiteren Standort in Kajaani an.
Googles Reaktion auf die unzulässige Rodung
Nach dem Schreiben der finnischen Aufsichtsbehörde vom 6. Oktober hat das Unternehmen die Arbeiten an beiden Standorten eingestellt und sich für die Rodungen entschuldigt. Der Finnland-Chef des Tech-Unternehmens, Antti Järvinen, erklärte einige Tage nach Erhalt des Schreibens, Google habe nach seinem damaligen Verständnis der Rechtslage gehandelt.
Zudem will Google nach eigenen Angaben die Wasserqualität am Standort Muhos schützen und auf 130 Hektar Bäume pflanzen. Naturschützer:innen halten diese Fläche jedoch für unzureichend, um im Vergleich zu den schon verursachten Schäden eine echte Wirkung zu erzielen, heißt es im Guardian.
Finnlands Rechenzentren
Mit 145 neuen Rechenzentren in verschiedenen Planungsphasen steht Finnland an der Spitze der jüngsten Offensive der Tech-Unternehmen. Das Land lockt mit vergleichsweise stabilen geopolitischen und geologischen Verhältnissen, reichlich Fläche und einem kühlen Klima, das die Energiekosten drücken kann.
Die Standorte in Muhos und Kajaani gehören zu Googles 13-Milliarden-Euro-Projekt für den Aufbau einer KI‑Infrastruktur. Es ist das größte Projekt dieser Art, das Finnland je erlebt hat. Die finnische Regierung hat tiefgreifende Sparmaßnahmen durchgesetzt, wirbt aber zugleich für die Investition: Als Google seine Pläne im vergangenen Monat vorstellte, bezeichnete Premierminister Petteri Orpo die Gewinnung von Investitionen als „höchste Priorität“ und dass der Deal „beiden Seiten dauerhafte Vorteile bringen“ würde.
In Finnland formiert sich jedoch Widerstand gegen den schnellen Ausbau von Rechenzentren. Kritiker:innen befürchten Schäden für Wälder, Gewässer und Tierwelt sowie Belastungen durch Lärm und steigende Energiepreise. Das enthüllte Fehlverhalten seitens Googles feuert die Debatte zusätzlich an. „Ich will sie hier nicht“, sagte eine Anwohnerin, die in der Nähe eines Rechenzentrums lebt, über Google. „Ich will sie überhaupt nicht in Finnland haben. Mir gefällt die ganze Idee der KI nicht, und auch nicht, wie sich die Welt verändert“, sagt sie gegenüber dem Guardian.

articles.title: Prêt pour GTA VI ? AliExpress affiche la PS5 Slim avec lecteur en promo pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Les Singles’ Day d’AliExpress ouvrent le mois du Black Friday, à trois semaines de la sortie de GTA VI, attendu le 19 novembre sur PS5. Avec le code FRD11120, la PS5 Slim blanche avec lecteur et 1 To y descend à 758,59 €, un prix qui reste supérieur de 108,60 € au tarif officiel de Sony en France.
La PS5 Slim avec lecteur est la version de la console de Sony qui lit encore les jeux sur disque. Le modèle proposé ici correspond à la révision dite châssis E, en coloris blanc, avec un SSD de 1 To et une manette DualSense. Sur AliExpress, elle passe à 758,59 € avec le code FRD11120, contre 878,59 € affichés par le vendeur, du 1er au 12 novembre.
Ce prix reste au-dessus des 649,99 € que Sony pratique en France depuis la hausse du 2 avril 2026. L’offre s’adresse donc surtout à ceux qui ne trouveraient pas la console à son tarif officiel chez les enseignes françaises.
La PS5 Slim avec lecteur et 1 To de stockage est à 758,59 € au lieu de 878,59 € chez AliExpress, une fois le code FRD11120 appliqué.
Pourquoi choisir la PS5 Slim avec lecteur ?
- Un lecteur de disque amovible : Il se retire sans le moindre outil en moins de dix secondes, comme nous l’avions vérifié. Vous gardez l’accès aux jeux physiques, neufs, prêtés ou d’occasion.
- 1 To de stockage : Nous avions relevé 822 Go disponibles au premier démarrage, contre 667 Go sur la PS5 d’origine. Un SSD supplémentaire jusqu’à 8 To peut s’ajouter quand la place vient à manquer.
- Une console qui se fait oublier : Notre test l’a jugée totalement imperceptible une fois en jeu. Elle occupe aussi environ 30 % de volume en moins que le premier modèle.
Jeux en boîte, GTA VI et salon : à qui sert cette version
La PS5 Slim offre exactement les mêmes performances que la PS5 d’origine, puisqu’elle reprend la même puce. Son intérêt tient à son format : plus compacte, plus légère, avec deux ports USB-C en façade. Le lecteur sert à ceux qui achètent leurs jeux en boîte, les revendent ou les échangent. La sortie de GTA VI, prévue le 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5 et Xbox Series, fait de novembre un mois où beaucoup de joueurs s’équipent.
Comme le résumait notre test de la PlayStation 5 Slim, notée 9/10, il s’agit d’une amélioration de format plus que d’une nouvelle console. Elle convient à un premier achat de PS5, installée sous le téléviseur du salon. En revanche, si vous possédez déjà une PS5 d’origine, rien ne justifie de changer : vous paieriez le même matériel une seconde fois. Et si vous n’achetez que des jeux dématérialisés, la version Digital, à 599,99 € au prix officiel, suffit.
AliExpress face au prix officiel de Sony : où se situe cette offre
Le vrai point de comparaison, ici, est le tarif officiel : 649,99 € pour la PS5 avec lecteur, 599,99 € pour la Digital et 899,99 € pour la PS5 Pro depuis avril. À 758,59 €, l’offre AliExpress se place à mi-chemin entre la Slim et la Pro au prix Sony. La remise de 120 € apportée par le code se calcule sur le prix affiché par le vendeur, pas sur un prix de marché. Autre détail utile : la version Digital du châssis E est passée à 825 Go, alors que la version avec lecteur conserve bien son 1 To.
✅ Les points forts
- Lecteur de disque amovible sans outil
- SSD de 1 To, extensible jusqu’à 8 To
- Console très discrète en jeu selon notre test
- Deux ports USB-C en façade
- Offre valable du 1er au 12 novembre, avant la sortie de GTA VI
❌ Les limites
- 108,60 € plus chère que le prix officiel de Sony
- Remise calculée sur le prix affiché par le vendeur
- Vendeur, origine et garantie à vérifier sur la fiche
- Aucun gain de performances face à la PS5 d’origine
Entre le 1er et le 12 novembre, le code FRD11120 ramène la PS5 Slim blanche à 758,59 € sur AliExpress, le temps de ses Singles’ Day.
Cette PS5 Slim à 758,59 € n’est pas une affaire au sens strict : le même modèle vaut 649,99 € au prix officiel de Sony. Le code FRD11120 rend l’offre moins chère que le prix affiché par le vendeur, sans la rendre compétitive face au tarif public. Elle n’a de sens que si les enseignes françaises n’affichent plus la console à son prix officiel au moment où vous commandez.
Avant de valider, comparez avec les prix pratiqués en France, qui peuvent bouger tout au long du mois, jusqu’au Black Friday du 27 novembre. Vérifiez aussi sur la fiche le vendeur, le pays d’expédition et la garantie : le libellé rédigé en anglais ne dit pas s’il s’agit d’une version européenne. Si vous n’êtes pas pressé, le Black Friday dira si la PS5 Slim repasse sous son tarif officiel, comme lors des éditions précédentes.

articles.title: Black Friday avant l'heure : Decathlon retire plus de 600 € à son VTT électrique tout suspendu, l'E-EXPL 520 S — Frandroid
articles.text:
Dans la gamme E-EXPL de Decathlon, le 520 S est le tout suspendu placé sous le E-EXPL 700 S (batterie de 630 Wh, 3 499,99 euros), face au E-EXPL 520, un semi-rigide à moteur Yamaha de 50 Nm. Il vise les randonnées sur chemins cassants, avec un dénivelé modéré. Decathlon a développé ce cadre en interne et l’a équipé d’un moteur Brose Drive T. Avec le Black Friday qui démarre en avance, le vélo est désormais disponible avec plus de 600 euros de remise.
Les atouts du Rockrider E-EXPL 520 S
- Un moteur central Brose Drive T de 70 Nm avec capteur de couple
- 140 mm de débattement à l’avant comme à l’arrière, signé X-Fusion
- Tige de selle télescopique et transmission MicroShift Advent X 10 vitesses
Affiché 2 999,99 euros en temps normal, le Rockrider E-EXPL 520 S descend à 2 398,99 euros chez Decathlon. Vous économisez donc 601 euros, soit 20 % de moins.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Rockrider E-EXPL 520 S. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un tout suspendu taillé pour les chemins cassants
Le cadre en aluminium 6061 adopte une architecture monopivot avec biellette. À l’avant, on trouve une fourche X-Fusion McQueen R. À l’arrière, un amortisseur X-Fusion O2 Pro R. Les deux offrent 140 mm de débattement. Sur des racines, des ornières ou une série de marches, ça change tout par rapport à un semi-rigide (vos poignets vous diront merci). Les roues de 29 pouces, chaussées de pneus Rockrider Grip 500, aident aussi à enjamber les obstacles sans trop se poser de questions.
La tige de selle télescopique est livrée de série, ce qui est loin d’être systématique à ce prix. Un coup de commande et paf, la selle s’efface avant la descente. Decathlon fournit aussi les éclairages, la sonnette, les catadioptres et les pédales, et le cadre est décliné en quatre tailles, du S au XL.
Un moteur Brose qui pousse sans brusquer
Le moteur central Brose Drive T développe 70 Nm de couple et monte jusqu’à 460 watts en pointe. Grâce à son capteur de couple, l’assistance suit l’effort de la jambe de façon progressive, sans à-coups au démarrage. Logé dans le pédalier, le moteur abaisse aussi le centre de gravité, ce qui rassure en descente. Comme l’impose la réglementation européenne des vélos à assistance électrique, l’assistance se coupe à 25 km/h.
La batterie de 500 Wh est intégrée au cadre, avec une sortie latérale pour la retirer. Le vélo se connecte aussi à l’application Decathlon Ride pour suivre vos sorties. Honnêtement, les 70 Nm restent en retrait face aux 100 Nm d’un Bosch Performance Line CX de dernière génération. Sur les rampes les plus raides et techniques, il faudra appuyer un peu plus fort sur les pédales. Pour de la randonnée avec un dénivelé modéré, c’est amplement suffisant.

articles.title: Cette impressionnante limousine Volkswagen à 24 000 € pourrait arriver en Europe
articles.text:
La surprise est encore meilleure que prévue. Alors que la Volkswagen ID. Unyx 09 débutait à 199 900 yuans en précommande, ses tarifs se révèlent être encore plus bas, à 179 900 yuans, soit environ 24 000 €. Aussi surprenante soit-elle, cette baisse est finalement nécessaire pour tenter de dévisser des rivales très compétitives. Mais au fait, qu’est-ce que l’ID. Unyx 09 ? Ce modèle étant parfaitement inconnu en Europe, des présentations s’imposent.
Inédite de la tête aux pieds, cette limousine électrique de 5,08 mètres étroitement développée avec Xpeng, doit chiper des clients aux stars du marché local. Outre un prix serré, l’auto joue sur une gamme simplifiée avec un équipement complet et une forte autonomie. Deux versions retenant une unique batterie de 92 kWh sont ainsi au programme. L’entrée de gamme en propulsion de 313 ch permet 755 km d’autonomie sur le cycle CLTC.
Une recharge ultra-rapide et des technologies de pointe : le grand atout technique
Le modèle bimoteur ajoute une machine électrique de 190 ch sur le train avant pour former une transmission intégrale. Le rayon d’action baisse alors à 705 km, toujours selon la norme CLTC. Côté recharge, Volkswagen profite du savoir-faire d’Xpeng en la matière avec une batterie 5C capable de se revigorer cinq fois en une heure. Concrètement, la marque annonce 250 km d’autonomie regagnés en 5 minutes de charge.
Entendez par là un 10 à 80 % de batterie en moins d’un quart d’heure. Côté équipement, l’ID. Unyx 09 retient les feux matriciels à LED capables de projeter des guides lumineux au sol, les jantes de 21 pouces cachant des étriers de freins Brembo, la puce Turing avec une puissance de calcul de 750 TOPS pour la conduite autonome et la suspension pneumatique à double chambre pour un confort accru.
À quel prix et quand pourrions-nous la voir en Europe ?
À bord, on dispose d’un écran tactile intégrant un assistant vocal commandé par intelligence artificielle, d’un affichage tête haute en réalité augmentée de 85 pouces, d’un volant à deux branches et d’une épaisse console centrale présentant un chargeur de smartphone sans fil. L’ambiance est classique et épurée, comme sur nombre de modèles concurrents. Bref, ce n’est pas à ce chapitre que l’ID. Unyx 09 étonnera. La grande nouvelle est en effet ailleurs.
Ce vaisseau spatial pourrait arriver chez nous, la marque envisageant d’exporter ses modèles chinois sur d’autres marchés. L’Australie et le Moyen-Orient auront la primeur de la chose, avant une éventuelle venue en Europe. L’ID. Unyx 09 se positionnera alors au sommet de la gamme, au-dessus même de la déjà imposante ID.7. Niveau prix, en revanche, les 24 000 € constitueront un rêve inaccessible. Comptez plutôt un tarif autour des 60 000 €…

articles.title: TVS Capital’s Rs 750-Cr private-credit bet
articles.text:
TVS Capital’s Rs 750-Cr private-credit bet; What makes people pay attention to content?
TVS Capital has launched TVS Alts, a private-credit platform targeting Rs 750 crore, with a green-shoe option lifting its potential corpus to Rs 1,250 crore.
Dear Reader,
The AI gold rush is running into a reality check, and the pressure is beginning to show across technology and crypto.
Anthropic’s much-anticipated Nasdaq debut is facing a tougher road after a week of market jitters over the cost of the AI boom. Its prospectus has impressed investors with reported annual sales growth of 1,300%, but its substantial computing commitments and losses have raised questions about whether surging demand can translate into a sustainable business.
Earnings from key partners Microsoft, Google and Amazon have added to the uncertainty, with massive infrastructure spending weighing on cash flow, even as cloud growth remains strong. Investors are now weighing the opportunity against the risks, just as Anthropic prepares for a potentially record-setting IPO.
The nerves have also reached OpenAI. According to The Financial Times, the ChatGPT maker has cut its latest funding target by $10 billion to around $20 billion, while lowering its desired valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion. The move comes amid a technology sell-off, with investors becoming more cautious about the huge sums being poured into AI.
Meanwhile, crypto has its own security headache. Following a reported $6.3 billion hack at Binance, rival exchanges including Coinbase and Kraken are strengthening their defences. Executives are also calling for faster information-sharing and coordinated responses, as the industry faces growing pressure to prove it can protect customers and stolen assets.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- TVS Capital’s Rs 750-crore private-credit bet
- What makes people pay attention to content?
Here’s your trivia for today: What was Google’s search engine originally called? (Scroll down for the answer)
Investment
TVS Capital’s Rs 750-crore private-credit bet
TVS Capital has launched TVS Alts, a private-credit platform targeting Rs 750 crore, with a green-shoe option lifting its potential corpus to Rs 1,250 crore. The fund awaits SEBI approval and will lend to performing firms, courting domestic institutions and corporates.
Key takeaways:
- The fund plans secured loans of Rs 40 crore to Rs 100 crore, targeting returns of about 17% and financing bridge needs, pre-IPO activity, mergers and acquisitions.
- TVS Capital owns 90% of the platform, while co-founder Shyam Srinivasan holds the rest and is leading the venture. Manish Makaria has been named Managing Partner.
- India’s private-credit market saw $3.5 billion invested across more than 100 deals in H1 2026. Domestic funds supplied 74% of deal value, amid fresh rival fundraises.
TechSparks
What makes people pay attention to content?
At TechSparks 2026, leaders from HT Media Labs, Inshorts, and Eloelo Group discussed why credibility, human creativity, and audience-first formats will matter as content creation scales.
The conversation explored how formats shape the way audiences consume content, what makes a format resonate in an increasingly crowded digital landscape, and why the format itself can be as important as the content it carries.
Key takeaways:
- Format, distribution, personalisation and the relationship with the consumer are congruent and they co-exist. All of them need to be married in a particular combination to get a person’s attention, said Avinash Mudaliar, Co-founder and CEO of HT Media Labs and the creator of the retro-styled portable music player Saregama Carvaan.
- Deepit Purkayastha, Co-founder and CEO of digital media and news aggregator company Inshorts, said while AI platforms are increasingly meeting consumers’ on-demand information needs, people still want real-time updates.
- For GSN Aditya, COO of entertainment tech company Eloelo Group, micro-drama economics have created opportunities to tell stories for more specific audiences rather than chase mass appeal.

articles.title: OpenAI says it's doubling Pro usage limits and bringing Work features to Chat
articles.text:
OpenAI has just confirmed that it's rolling out ChatGPT Work capabilities directly into regular Chat, while also combining usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex.
In an email seen by BleepingComputer, OpenAI noted that it will test a combined experience for Chat and Work tabs in the coming weeks, initially with a small group of users.
If you're selected for the test, you'll be able to move from ordinary conversations to more complex tasks without switching modes.
"This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place," OpenAI explained.
"You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work."
The combined experience will initially be tested with a small group of users before OpenAI expands it to more people.
It is worth noting that Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.
ChatGPT and Codex will share the same usage allowance
There's another significant change coming to Pro subscriptions. OpenAI is preparing to unify usage across ChatGPT and Codex, meaning both services will draw from the same allowance.
"Your use of ChatGPT and Codex will draw from the same allowance," OpenAI noted in the email.
However, not every conversation will consume that allowance. OpenAI says Unlimited Instant is included in the subscription and won't count towards the shared usage limit.
More advanced models and complex tasks will consume more of your allowance, depending on the work involved.
You'll also be able to check your combined remaining usage and reset times under Settings > Usage:
If you run out, you can wait for the allowance to reset, upgrade your subscription, or purchase credits for eligible features.
Separately, OpenAI has already doubled Work and Codex allowances for its Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500 subscriptions, effective October 29.

articles.title: Los bancos comunitarios demandan al regulador de EE. UU. por las licencias de empresas de criptomonedas
articles.text:
La Asociación de Bancos Comunitarios de EE. UU. (Independent Community Bankers of America, o ICBA) ha demandado a la Oficina del Interventor de la Moneda (OCC), el regulador federal de los bancos nacionales.
El caso se tramita en el tribunal federal de distrito de Washington D.C. y acusa a la OCC de excederse en sus facultades legales al permitir que empresas de criptomonedas obtengan licencias de banco fiduciario nacional. La mayoría de los miembros de la asociación tienen activos inferiores a 10.000 millones de dólares.
Demandan que anulen una regla de la OCC y su carta interpretativa 1176. Piden además que el tribunal declare que son ilegales. Que la OCC no pueda seguir aplicando esas dos normas para otorgar nuevas licencias y que se anule la aprobación de una concreta (Protego Holdings).
En palabras de su presidenta y CEO, Rebeca Romero Rainey, en un comunicado: “Los consumidores estadounidenses tienen legítimamente expectativas de que las entidades bancarias con licencias federales tengan protección federal. Los activos digitales en posesión de empresas cripto que tienen licencias fiduciarias nacionales no cuentan con esas importantes garantías”.
La regla de la OCC y la carta 1176
La regla fue publicada el 2 de marzo de 2026 y entró en vigor el 1 de abril. Entre otras cosas, modifica el reglamento de licencias. Se cambia el término “actividades fiduciarias” por “operaciones de una compañía fiduciaria y actividades relacionadas”. Además, en el propio boletín en el que presenta la regla, la OCC asegura que esta “no aumenta ni disminuye” su autoridad para otorgar licencias.
Esta es la visión de ICBA. En la demanda también se afirma que la enmienda de 1978 solo permite limitar el banco nacional a ser compañía fiduciaria. Por ello, solo pueden autorizarse tres tipos de banco nacional: los que aceptan depósitos, los que prestan servicios a otros bancos y los fiduciarios. Esa ampliación de poderes, dice el texto, generaría “un enorme vacío en la regulación financiera”.
A los que usan plataformas de criptomonedas les interesa saber qué pasa con el seguro. La demanda indica que los bancos fiduciarios (que no aceptan depósitos) están excluidos de buena parte de la regulación federal. Sus clientes no tienen seguro de depósitos. En una de sus fichas orientadas al ciudadano de 2022, la Corporación Federal de Seguro de Depósitos (FDIC) explica que su seguro solo cubre los depósitos en bancos asegurados y no se aplica a los criptoactivos.
Protego y las licencias aprobadas hasta ahora
Se trata de la compañía cuya aprobación quiere anular ICBA. Protego planea cuatro líneas de negocio distintas. Custodia, plataforma de trading, plataforma en la que unos clientes prestan sus criptomonedas custodiadas a otros clientes. Y servicios de emisión de tokens.
Es una aprobación preliminar. En los tres primeros años deberá tener un mínimo de 15 millones de dólares de capital de nivel 1. También deberá tener 180 días de gastos de funcionamiento en activos líquidos. Mientras no se otorgue la definitiva, la OCC puede modificar o anular esta aprobación. ICBA, que se opuso a la licencia, alega que la OCC ha ignorado los avisos de que Protego tenía funciones de riesgo y control con graves fallos. También que tenía un problema de gobernanza (sin supervisión independiente).
En la era Trump, según la demanda, la OCC ha aprobado o dado visto bueno a 21 licencias de banco fiduciario nacional. Al menos 13 corresponden a compañías de criptos. En un comunicado indicaba que tenía en su cartera unas 60 de estas entidades. Dio visto bueno condicionado a cinco más (Ripple National Trust Bank, BitGo y Paxos entre ellos).
Xataka ya informó de que diez de los mayores bancos del mundo estaban explorando poner en marcha sus propias stablecoins. Entre ellos se encontraban Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Santander o BNP Paribas.
El 26 de octubre de 2026 (ya tras la demanda), Ripple ha anunciado en un comunicado que la OCC le da la aprobación final para lanzar su banco fiduciario. Este gestionará las reservas de su stablecoin RLUSD. También ofrecerá servicios de custodia de activos digitales. RLUSD se emite desde una compañía fiduciaria regulada en Nueva York. El asunto es si el tribunal admite la interpretación de la ley de 1978 que defiende ICBA.

articles.title: Europe and Canada team up in AI computing alliance that doesn't depend on Washington
articles.text:
Sour Syrup: Geopolitical relations between Canada and the US are fraying fast, and Europe could capitalize by deepening its partnership with the proud North American nation. The new partners will likely need a lot of money, however, to make a real dent against US-based HPC powerhouses.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen recently confirmed that Canada is joining Europe's network of supercomputers, which is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking. Canada will become an active part of the public-private network of high-performance computing (HPC) systems, and both sides should gain something from the arrangement, at least in theory.
Von der Leyen said the new cooperation will give Canadian industry privileged access to Europe's supercomputing resources, and startups and research organizations will also be able to join in. The European Union, meanwhile, will be able to tap Canada's competitive tech industry to further expand the shared AI ecosystem.
The EuroHPC network includes 14 world-class supercomputers, 10 quantum computers, and 19 "AI factories." Its umbrella covers 67 research projects, 38 participating countries, and 36 national competence centers. EuroHPC's total budget is €8.2 billion, while a further €30 billion investment is expected to add up to seven new AI data centers, with construction starting next year.
Anton Leicht, an AI expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, called cooperation among "middle powers" such as Canada and the EU one of the most obvious short-term moves toward a common AI infrastructure. He warned, however, that the new HPC-focused relationship will likely have no practical effect on US interests and dominance in the supercomputer business.
Washington will still hold significant sway over both Canada and the EU, Leicht suggested, because the US is making its own massive investments in new HPC and AI data center capacity.
"As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," Leicht said.
Either way, Canada is making a significant effort to become one of Europe's most privileged partners. Prime Minister Mark Carney and von der Leyen have recently launched an Alliance for the Future, opening a new avenue for "like-minded nations" to tackle common issues.
Von der Leyen has floated making Canada the EU's first associate member, with joint HPC resources just one part of a larger initiative that is likely to rankle the US administration.

articles.title: FBI Links North Korea's TraderTraitor to Record $6.43 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
articles.text:
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-aligned elite hacking group also tracked as Jade Sleet, Pressure Chollima, PUKCHONG, Slow Pisces, and UNC4899.
The FBI, along with the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), said it observed the threat actor converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH).
"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement.
The agency has also provided a list of wallet addresses that the attackers are said to be using to launder the stolen assets.
The development comes as Binance said it has resumed phase one of withdrawals starting today between 6 and 9 a.m. UTC after they were paused in the wake of the incident.
"Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services," Binance said in a statement.
"We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks. Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident."
The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin.
"This single incident almost doubles the total cryptoassets stolen by the regime," blockchain analysis firm Elliptic said. "Actors linked to North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), are believed to have stolen over $6.5 billion in cryptoassets in recent years."
Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.
TraderTraitor is the name assigned to a North Korean group that has a history of orchestrating cryptocurrency thefts against the Web3.0 industry by tricking victims into downloading malware-laced applications. The cluster is known to be active since at least 2020.
In recent years, the adversary has been attributed to cryptocurrency heists targeting DMM Bitcoin, Bybit, KelpDAO, and Bitget.
Reports from SentinelOne, Zscaler ThreatLabz, and Microsoft have revealed that TraderTraitor is continuing to hone its tradecraft, using trojanized Terraform providers as a malware distribution vector and leveraging front companies to conduct job-themed targeting against individuals involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies.
The poisoned Terraform provider is used to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. This includes a cross-platform implant called FLATROOF, which siphons sensitive data from the victim using a Python-based information stealer before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to obtain complete remote control.
The activity once again demonstrates how North Korean threat actors continue to abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems, and gain persistent access.
TraderTraitor's modus operandi, like other North Korea-linked campaigns such as Lazarus Group's Operation Dream Job and Famous Chollima's Contagious Interview, employs recruitment-themed lures as a pretext to convince victims to run malicious code. The social engineering phase is augmented by the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to craft convincing lures, create fake personas, and evade detection.
"The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach," Microsoft said.
"Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge."

articles.title: Agentic AI architecture demands real-time databases - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Agent demand can’t be forecast, meaning the database has to be ready for anything
Enterprises building an agentic AI architecture are learning that the database matters as much as the model. AI agents fire off thousands of unplanned queries at once — and expect answers in milliseconds.
PhoenixAI, the trade name of CelerData Inc., raised $80 million this year to develop database technology for AI agents to solve this growing problem. Established players struggle to return answers in real time, according to Ross Armstrong (pictured), senior vice president of global sales of PhoenixAI.
“There was a real gap in the market for real-time analytics, and to be able to not only ask a question but get the response back in real time was something that all the database players that are out there, even the big names in the market, couldn’t do well,” Armstrong said. “If you have customer-facing analytics or agentic AI … you need that response time to be able to meet the SLAs with your customers.”
Armstrong spoke with theCUBE’s Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the database demands of agentic AI, real-time query performance and the need for governance and observability. (* Disclosure below.)
Building an agentic AI architecture for unpredictable demand
Agents generate queries in real time and may hit several databases at once, according to Armstrong. PhoenixAI’s specific columnar engine handles structured and unstructured data and works out how to answer each query as it arrives.
“I think what the biggest demand is that we don’t know what the demand is going to be from those agents,” Armstrong said. “You could have … thousands and thousands of queries hitting at the exact same time, but you still need that real speedy response.”
PhoenixAI joined Cloudera as a foundational database partner and is now an option in Cloudera’s marketplace. Its self-managed edition, PhoenixAI Anywhere, runs in a customer’s cloud, on-premises or in air-gapped environments. In a market where many early adopters hit governance and observability problems, PhoenixAI plans to address them with AgentBase, a purpose-built context environment that keeps agents away from data they don’t need, Armstrong explained.
“You can design that playground for those agents to be protected and to be governed but also to give them access to the data that you need,” Armstrong said. “It’s not necessary to run agents on a solution like PhoenixAI, but it’s certainly one that helps you put those guardrails in that a lot of organizations are looking for.”

articles.title: Amazons neue Echos: Alexa am Bett und eine Kamera fürs Wohnzimmer
articles.text:
Amazons neue Echos: Alexa am Bett und eine Kamera fürs Wohnzimmer
Spot, Dot, Show, Studio. Wer alle Echo-Lautsprecher von Amazon aufzählen können will, braucht mittlerweile ein gutes Gedächtnis, denn die Geräte kommen in zahlreichen Varianten und Größen. Mit dem Echo Time kommt jetzt ein weiterer Speaker mit Zugriff auf Alexa hinzu. Der soll nach den Vorstellungen des Versandhändlers vor allem als smarter Wecker auf dem Nachtisch eine gute Figur machen.
Echo Time weckt zur besten Zeit
Deswegen ist der Echo auch mit einem Set an Sensoren ausgestattet. Der Hersteller spricht dabei von „Omnisense“. Anhand von Raumtemperatur und Präsenzerkennung soll der smarte Speaker die Schlafroutine erfassen, via Ultraschall die Atmung erkennen. Eine Kamera ist ausdrücklich nicht verbaut. Mithilfe der Daten soll Echo Time Nutzer:innen im optimalen Moment, also in einer leichten Schlafphase, aufwecken. Dies geschieht innerhalb von zehn bis 60 Minuten in der eingestellten Weckzeit.
Für typische Snooze-Drücker hat sich Amazon ein, zwei Tricks ausgedacht: So sollen Klingeltöne auf Wunsch nach jedem „Schlummern“ lauter werden. Bis zu viermal sei das möglich. Das verbaute, 3,2 Zoll große, Display könne zudem einen Sonnenaufgang simulieren, indem es zur Weckzeit stetig heller wird. Ob das bei der Größe eine echte Hilfe ist, bleibt abzuwarten. Nachts soll der Bildschirm zumindest nicht stören, weil er die Helligkeit dimmt, den Blaulichtanteil senkt und nur noch die Uhr- und Weckzeit anzeigt. Über Tag (also, wenn sich niemand im Schlafzimmer befindet) zeigt Echo Time auf Wunsch eines von hunderten Uhrendesigns ab.
Herzstück des smarten Weckers soll, wie bei allen neuen Lautsprechern, natürlich Alexa Plus sein. Die Assistenz auf KI-Basis soll mehrere Befehle aus einer Anfrage erkennen und umsetzen können. Neben einer normalen gibt es außerdem eine Kinderfunktion, bei der Eltern die Kontrolle über den Zugriff auf die Inhalte behalten.
Echo Dot ist jetzt ein Smarthome-Gateway
Darüber hinaus stellt Amazon eine neue Version des Echo Dot vor. Es soll sich um die bislang leistungsstärkste Ausgabe des kleinen Lautsprechers handeln. Das liegt am verbauten AZ3-Chip, der Anfragen direkt auf dem Gerät bearbeiten kann und so für ein besseres Gesprächserlebnis mit Alexa sorgen soll. Welche Daten genau direkt auf dem Speaker verarbeitet werden, verrät Amazon allerdings nicht.
Drei Extras sollen den Dot aber von seinen Vorgängern abheben: Er enthält jetzt ein viertes Mikrofon, mit dem er laut Hersteller Befehle über den Raum hinweg besser wahrnehmen kann. Erstmals ist auch ein Smarthome-Hub integriert. Damit lassen sich Geräte ohne die Bridges oder Gateways von Drittanbietern direkt mit dem Lautsprecher verbinden. In WLAN-Netzwerken von Amazons Eero-Routern kann der Dot außerdem als Repeater fungieren, um die Reichweite zu erhöhen.
Echo Studio jetzt mit Kamera
Außerdem erweitert ein neuer Echo Studio mit eingebauter Kamera, aber ohne Bildschirm das Lineup. Mithilfe der Knipse sollt ihr von der visuellen Intelligenz von Alexa Plus profitieren. Allerdings löst die Kamera wohl eher Probleme, die nur wenige haben. Ein Beispielcase des Herstellers: Haltet ein Brettspiel vor die Linse und Alexa kann euch die Regeln erklären. Zusätzlich soll die Assistenz damit etwa Lebensmittel erkennen und bei der Bestellung helfen.
Eine physische Blende zur Abdeckung der Kamera gibt es offenbar nicht. Stattdessen verweist der Hersteller auf die übliche Taste, die die Mikrofone stummschalten kann. Diese gelte dann auch für die Kamera. Immerhin soll das Gerät aber über visuelle Signale klarmachen, wann es Bilder und Videos in die Cloud lädt.
Der Echo Dot kostet 104,99 Euro, die Kinderversion ist zehn Euro teurer. Für den Echo Studio mit Kamera werden 259,99 Euro fällig. Echo Time kostet euch 214,99 Euro (224,99 Euro für Kinder). Alle Modelle sind ab sofort erhältlich. Ein günstigerer Zeitpunkt zum Einkauf dürfte allerdings die nahende Black-Friday-Woche sein. In der Regel senkt Amazon seine eigene Hardware dann stark im Preis.

articles.title: Open-source security in the AI exploit era: Patch without changing a thing
articles.text:
Open-source security in the AI exploit era: Patch without changing a thing
Here’s how a vulnerability in a popular open-source library plays out in 2026: A maintainer merges a fix and publishes an advisory. Within hours, someone points a model at the diff between the old and new versions and gets a working exploit back. Your scanner flags the CVE the next morning, a ticket gets filed, and the fix is scheduled into next week’s change window. By then the exploit has been circulating for days.
That was a fine enterprise lifestyle choice last year, but it’s considered out of fashion nowadays.
And for good reason, as Michael Cembalest goes over in his “Patchmageddon” report from July 2026, which includes input from J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s cybersecurity leadership. Models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT–5.5 now find previously unknown vulnerabilities at a scale no human research team can match. Anthropic and its Project Glasswing partners found more than 10,000 new high- and critical-severity zero-days in the first month alone.
At the same time, the exploitation clock shrank. The note puts the median time from disclosure to first exploitation at roughly a year in 2021. Now it’s down to one day in 2026, and projected to be one minute by 2027. Almost 80% of exploitations now land on or before their public disclosure. Models can find vulnerabilities, and hackers can exploit them just as fast, if not faster.
Open source takes the first hit
That pressure lands on open source first, because open source is what modern software is made of and because the source is, well, open for all to see. This is fantastic, and as it should be: it just means it’s the low-hanging fruit for hackers.
The people expected to absorb this flood of AI-driven vulnerabilities are mostly volunteers. Of 530 high- and critical-severity findings Anthropic reported to open source maintainers by May 2026, only 75 had been patched. This past summer was filled with open source maintainers closing down bug bounty programs and putting up the gone fishing sign to de-stress.
Your new security strategy
Like it or not, corporate mindsets about security tend to shift when there’s urgency and a touch of, well, worry. Here’s some more freak-out fuel:
- More models are getting better – Cembalest’s note expects capabilities now confined to a handful of nation-state units to be reproducible in freely available open-weight models within 12 to 24 months. Hamish Low at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy gives a Chinese Mythos-class model a 40% chance by February 2027 and near-certainty by the end of that year.
- You’re already running vulnerable code, probably – most of what you run was pulled from public registries months ago, if not years. Datadog’s February 2026 numbers put TK{spell this out in plainer language // the median dependency 278 days behind its latest major version}. That’s old code waiting for a one-day exploit.
- The yardstick has changed – Cembalest is blunt that organizations will have to judge themselves on patching speed, not just accuracy. Programs built around 90-day disclosure windows are now measured against a clock that runs in hours.
If you own a platform, run application security, or sign off on technology risk in a regulated industry, this problem is circling you whether you act or not. Urgency without a plan is like listening to your seatmate on a five-hour-late flight rapidly text back and forth, with that duck quack at max volume for each message they receive. Annoying and a bit of a vibe killer.
To de-quackify, let us share the plan Oren has been sharing with platform and security leaders across financial services.
Stop building your security strategy around free beer
Not enough people work on open source to patch it fast enough.
Cembalest spends serious time on maintainer concentration. In a Linux Foundation and Harvard study of the top 50 open source projects, 23% had a single developer responsible for more than 80% of lines added, and 94% had fewer than ten developers writing more than 90% of the code. At registry level, Anchore counted more than 18 million npm packages listing a single maintainer.
“Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them.”
Most communities that write and support open source are doing the best they can, and many have burned out doing even more. But the promise of “free as in beer” was never that they’d keep you perfectly secure and deliver day-zero patches. The promise was, well, free beer. Enterprises have enjoyed decades of free beer – open source software – while being told it was sort of irresponsible of them. Now we’re seeing proof of that, in an entirely self-inflicted way. It’s time to pay for the beer.
This is where professional open source comes in. Yes, it means – take a deep breath and close your spreadsheets – paying to use freely downloadable software.
Professional open source is backed by a vendor with skin in the game, or a foundation with staffed security response, funded maintainers, and a release process that survives burnout. The team that creates and knows the code owns the fix and works under an SLA.
“If you can’t name who maintains a package, you can’t count on anyone to fix it.”
J.P. Morgan’s own technology leadership, summarized in Cembalest’s note, is explicit: run current versions, and move off dependencies where you can’t identify who maintains them, where the maintainer looks like a one-person shop, or where the package appears abandoned. If you can’t name who maintains a package, you can’t count on anyone to fix it.
Applying security patches is keeping the business running
Erik Scales, who leads platform engineering for Tanzu Platform at Charles Schwab, put it bluntly in a VMware Explore talk this year:
If you’ve ever tried to patch a server, no one wants to patch anything. No one wants to do anything. Now, everybody’s worried about being on the news and being fired.
The usual reason for putting off a patch is that the business has to keep running. A patch might break something, so it waits for the next change window, or the one after that. The J.P. Morgan note cites research finding that over 80% of security professionals have skipped a patch to avoid disrupting the business.
“Now that they show up within a day of disclosure, the unpatched system is the bigger threat to keeping the business running.”
When exploits took months to show up, that trade was defensible. Now that they show up within a day of disclosure, the unpatched system is the bigger threat to keeping the business running.
That still leaves the disruption problem. Any fix that adds a second disruption on top of the risk will get deferred too, and deferral is exactly what a one-day clock punishes. Attackers are counting on waiting.
Make the right thing the easiest thing
Control where your open source comes from, even more tightly than you do now.
We’re long past the days when enterprise developers could download anything from the internet and use it. A lot of hard work went into changing that habit. Most large companies now send every dependency download through an internal artifact proxy, like JFrog Artifactory or Sonatype Nexus. Developers point their builds at the proxy, and the proxy fetches from Maven Central, npm, or PyPI. Going through the slog of getting developers to change their habits again is not a good idea, nor, you know, fun.
You don’t have to. To change where your open source comes from, you change where the proxy fetches from, and nothing else. Point it at a supported source like TrueSource, and the build files, URLs, and pipelines all stay the same. Developers won’t notice a difference. What’s different is that the Spring libraries coming through now include fixes that often ship before the CVE is public.
The proxy can also do some of the patching for you. Set it to block known-vulnerable versions and serve the nearest patched one instead, and builds keep working without anyone filing a ticket. The patched package becomes the default, the one developers get without asking for it.
This is critical for how you address Patchmageddon. Changing developer habits is difficult once they are set in their ways. Because you can simply point the repositories at a proxy, you don’t have to change developer habits.
Oren has worked with large financial services platform teams that already run their dependencies through a proxy like this. For them, the conversation isn’t about pushing a new supply chain platform through the organization. It’s about pointing the proxy somewhere new, and that’s easy to do.
This is why we say the only acceptable change is no change.
The rest of the plan
Those are the big ones, and for some, the most difficult. There are three more items to consider as well:
- Measure how fast fixes reach production. Track the time from disclosure to a deployed fix for your top 50 dependencies. That’s the number the J.P. Morgan note says you’ll be judged on.
- Know who maintains your critical dependencies. For each one, write down the organization behind it. Single-maintainer and abandoned packages go on their own list.
- Use AI to find and propose fixes, and keep people on the merge. Ideally, those people are the code’s maintainers.
Security is different now, in a big, new way. Pay attention to it and adapt your organization’s security strategy. This is especially true if, like most large organizations and especially financial institutions, you develop and run a lot of your own software. We’ve shared what we think is a good plan to follow. Whether you like our plan or not, make sure you do something. And tell us how it goes.

articles.title: Northstar Security Exits Stealth With $7M to Expose Toxic Risk Combinations
articles.text:
Northstar Security, a startup developing AI agents for security teams, has emerged from stealth mode with $7 million in seed funding.
Wing Venture Capital led the round. MVP, Outliers, and cybersecurity veterans Gerhard Eschelbeck, Renaud Deraison, and Justin Somaini also invested.
The company ingests data from existing security and IT tools to build what it calls a Security Context Graph. Updated in real time, the graph shows how identities, assets, applications, vulnerabilities, and business systems connect to one another.
Northstar aims to catch so-called toxic combinations. Issues such as a vulnerability, an unmanaged device, or an account with excessive privileges may seem under control on their own, but together they can expose critical business systems.
For instance, the platform could flag a laptop lacking endpoint protection whose owner is a privileged user able to reach a critical payroll system.
Analysts can investigate findings like this by asking questions in plain language. Northstar’s agents can then kick off fixes, such as installing endpoint protection, notifying the user, or limiting their access, and people can supervise those actions where appropriate.
Customers can also give external AI agents access to the graph through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and build their own security workflows. Northstar says it connects to more than 70 enterprise security and IT products, among them Okta, GitHub, Workday, Microsoft Defender and Entra, AWS, and Google Cloud.
“Security teams are drowning in data but starving for context,” said Amer Deeba, Northstar’s CEO and co-founder.
Deeba co-founded Normalyze, which Proofpoint later acquired, and was previously a senior executive at Qualys. His co-founder, CTO Ed Rowe, held the same role at Farmers Business Network and led engineering as an SVP at AppDynamics.
The startup will use the money to develop its platform, hire staff, and expand its go-to-market push.

articles.title: NetamLoader Malware Targets Government Windows 10 Systems in Asia via .NET Injection
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia.
The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader.
The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information.
The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive (CAB) file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages.
It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software.
The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts.
Put differently, the approach targets .NET Framework's application-domain initialization to achieve code execution. The end result is the same as DLL sideloading: to run malicious code inside a legitimate application's process so as to fly under the radar.
According to Kaspersky, the CAB archive containing the .config file was placed in the path: "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24," with its contents extracted and dropped into "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\."
| Infection chain: Stage 1 | 
The exact delivery vehicle for the CAB archive remains unknown. Present in the archive are seven files, four of which are legitimate components of Patch My PC, an endpoint management software -
- fabric.config
- Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll
- PatchMyPC-Enum.dll
- PatchMyPC-Models.dll
- PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe
- PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config
- Resources.resx
None of the files with the exception of "Resources.resx" embed malicious code. The infection chain plays out as a two-stage process as follows -
- The execution of "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe" serves as the launchpad for several payloads. It abuses AppDomainManager injection to parse "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config," resulting in the execution of "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll."
- Once loaded, "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll" finds "fabric.config" located in the same directory and parses its contents to load "Resources.resx."
- "Resources.resx" contains "multiple layers" of encoded, compressed, or encrypted payloads, such as XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data, which are decoded and loaded by the component before it.
| Infection chain: Stage 2 | 
A brief description of these payloads is listed below -
- XAML-1, a loader for an embedded payload, XAML-2.
- XAML‑2 initializes the second stage of the attack chain by loading two compressed and Base64‑encoded XAML files: XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2. XAML-2-1 is used to bypass Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).
- XAML-2-2 contains two parts, a .NET module (aka .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (aka JSON-1).
- JSON-1, the JSON payload that contains two components: JSON-1-c, which stores command-and-control (C2) server configuration, and JSON-1-p, which contains a Base64‑encoded file (.NET 2 Plugin) and a collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3.
- XAML-2-2 loads .NET 1 Loader, which then serves as a decrypting, assembling, and loading for XAML‑3, reports the status to the C2 server, and deletes malicious files extracted from the CAB archive, along with CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to cover up the tracks.
- XAML-3, the XAML payload that runs within "dllhost.exe" and is designed to decode, decompress, and load .NET 2 Plugin.
- .NET 2 Plugin, a .NET assembly that loads the C2 configuration, gathers system information from Windows Registry, checks if the current host process is "dllhost.exe," waits a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes before issuing its first request to the C2 server ("openaigpt4v[.]com"), and enters into a periodic polling loop to fetch an XAML file and execute it in an isolated AppDomain.
"If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed," Kaspersky explained.
Telemetry data gathered by Kaspersky has identified a single victim in Asia, with NetamLoader designed to attack a Windows 10 build customized for government-only use. Although the targeted Asian country was not disclosed, signs are that it's likely China, as Microsoft offers a bespoke version called Windows 10 China Government Edition specifically for the Chinese government and state-owned entities.
Earlier this August, Bloomberg reported that China's Ministry of State Security had ordered some government agencies to stop using the "Government Edition" in favor of Chinese-made Linux distributions as part of an effort to reduce its dependence on foreign technology.
"Beijing's instruction stemmed from data security concerns," Bloomberg said, citing "people familiar with the matter." No additional details were disclosed at the time.
"In today's geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority," Kaspersky concluded.
"The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process."

articles.title: Un solo hombre frente a los ciberataques que tumbaron miles de webs: “Hace falta querer hacer algo por los demás”
articles.text: Ondrej Surý, ingeniero checo de 49 años y voluntario que mantiene los paquetes de PHP que usan millones de servidores de todo el mundo, en una imagen facilitada por él mismo. El discreto ingeniero checo Ondrej Surý, de 49 años, tiene 273 seguidores en la red social Mastodon y esta semana estaba de vacaciones en Italia. Tiene también un perfil en la plataforma Patreon en el que 490 personas le dan 1.539 euros mensuales. Allí se describe con estas palabras complejas: “Soy el principal empaquetador de PHP para Debian y de otros paquetes”. Bajo esos oscuros conceptos de software se esconde un trabajo voluntario que la semana pasada salvó millones de webs en todo el mundo. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: NVIDIA Updates Rubin GPU Specs as First Production Hardware Arrives
articles.text:
As we roll into the fourth quarter of 2026, NVIDIA and its partners are in the middle of the Vera Rubin ramp-up, including hyperscalers making some of the first NVL72 systems generally available to their customers. With Vera Rubin reaching the tipping point of its production roll-out, NVIDIA is also finally locking down the hardware shipping specifications. As it turns out, the company has quietly revised those specifications, with the Rubin GPU now offering less memory and scale-up networking (NVLink) bandwidth than NVIDIA previously promoted, but more scale-out bandwidth.
As initially spotted by IT Home, back in September NVIDIA posted the updated specifications for its Rubin GPU and various Rubin-based products on their webpages and in NVIDIA’s architecture datasheet. To be sure, it is not unusual for server hardware specifications to change before a product’s launch, especially for something like Vera Rubin, which was announced nearly a year in advance. NVIDIA’s case is no different, with the company previously noting that those specifications were preliminary and that “all values are up to and subject to change” at the time.
Rubin GPU: Less HBM4 Bandwidth, Less NVLink Bandwidth, More Scale-Out Bandwidth
First, let us talk about NVIDIA’s Rubin GPU. The cornerstone of NVIDIA’s ambitions for this generation, NVIDIA’s Rubin server GPU will find its way into systems big and small and serve as the building block for much larger projects.
| NVIDIA Rubin GPU Specifications |  |  |  |  | 
|  | Preliminary | Shipping |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Inference | 50 PFLOPS | 50 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Training | 35 PFLOPS | 35 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| INT8 | 250 TOPS | 250 TOPS |  |  | 
| TF32 | 2 PFLOPS | 2 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| GPU Memory | 288GB HBM4 (8x36GB) | 288GB HBM4 (8x36GB) |  |  | 
| GPU Memory Bandwidth | 22TB/sec (8×2048@10.75Gbps) | 19.2TB/sec (8×2048@9.375Gbps) |  |  | 
| NVLink Bandwidth (Scale Up) | 3.6TB/sec | 3.0TB/sec |  |  | 
| Networking Bandwidth (Scale Out) | 0.4TB/sec | 0.45TB/sec |  |  | 
| Architecture | Rubin | Rubin |  |  | 
Compared to NVIDIA’s preliminary specifications, the HBM4 memory bandwidth for a single Rubin GPU has been revised down notably. NVIDIA was initially targeting 22TB/second of memory bandwidth per Rubin GPU. At 8 stacks of HBM4 memory, that meant running each stack at about 10.75Gbps/pin. But with these revised shipping specifications, a single Rubin GPU will now provide 19.2TB/second of bandwidth, for a data rate of about 9.375Gbps/pin, a net loss of 1.375Gbps, or roughly 11%.
This spec change comes as NVIDIA has been projecting some very aggressive data rates for HBM4. The super-sized version of the high-bandwidth memory specification already doubled the memory bus width per stack from 1024 bits to 2048 bits. At the same time, the official specification called for HBM4 stacks to run at a slightly lower clock rate than HBM3E, targeting 8Gbps/pin. NVIDIA’s 10.75Gbps rate was significantly higher than the original HBM4 specification, and even their newly reduced 9.375Gbps data rate is still quite a bit above.
For context, NVIDIA’s rival AMD will run its HBM4 stacks on the MI455X at only 7.6Gbps/pin. So NVIDIA’s revised targets are significantly higher than those of some other HBM4 consumers. Even after the news broke, NVIDIA has not said why it revised the memory bandwidth specs down. In lieu of that, the immediate assumption is that NVIDIA and its memory partners cannot deliver on those specs, be it memory controller speeds, memory stack speeds, memory stack yields (how many can run at the desired speed), or perhaps a combination of all of those factors. Regardless of the reason, the net result is that customers will have less GPU memory bandwidth at their disposal, with performance ramifications.
NVLink interconnect bandwidth is also taking a hit compared to NVIDIA’s original expectations. The preliminary specification for NVIDIA’s multi-GPU connection and scale-up fabric was for 3.6TB/second of NVLink bandwidth for each Rubin GPU. That is now a flat 3.0TB/second, a 600GB/second (or 17%) reduction. NVLink is an area where NVIDIA pushes hard to make many physical GPUs act as one, so it usually pushes the limits of what is possible.
While NVLink (scale-up) bandwidth has been reduced, scale-out networking bandwidth is now overperforming. For a single Rubin GPU, NVIDIA is offering 450GB/second of networking bandwidth, up from their preliminary specification of 400GB/second.
Beyond these changes, NVIDIA has not changed any other specifications for Rubin GPUs. The theoretical (on paper) compute throughput remains unchanged at 50 PFLOPS of FP4 inference and 35 PFLOPS of FP4 training. So NVIDIA has hit its clock speed and memory-capacity targets for the GPU.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72: Rackscale Revised Accordingly
Rubin’s spec changes will also affect all the products it will go into, most notably NVIDIA’s flagship Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. NVL72 showcases all of NVIDIA’s technologies, integrating its Vera CPUs, BlueField-4 DPUs, and, of course, Rubin GPUs.
| NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Specifications |  |  |  |  | 
|  | Preliminary | Shipping |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Inference | 3600 PFLOPS | 50 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Training | 2520 PFLOPS | 35 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| INT8 | 18 POPS | 250 TOPS |  |  | 
| TF32 | 144 PFLOPS | 2 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| GPU Memory | 20.7TB HBM4 | 20.7TB HBM4 |  |  | 
| GPU Memory Bandwidth | 1580TB/sec | 1400TB/sec |  |  | 
| NVLink Bandwidth (Scale Up) | 260TB/sec | 216TB/sec |  |  | 
| Networking Bandwidth (Scale Out) | 28.8TB/sec | 32.4TB/sec |  |  | 
For NVL72, its specifications have been revised in lockstep with the changes to a single Rubin GPU. That means that cumulative GPU memory bandwidth has gone from 1,580TB/second to 1400TB/second for the rack-scale system, a net loss of 180 TB (11%). Though, as with a single Rubin, the GPU memory capacity for NVL72 remains unchanged at 20.7TB of HBM4.
NVLink bandwidth across the system for its scale-up domain has also been adjusted. NVIDIA’s plans to offer 260TB/second of bandwidth across the rack have been revised down to 216TB/second, a 17% reduction matching the new 3TB/second rate of each Rubin GPU.
The silver lining for NVL72 is that it gets the same scale-out networking bandwidth boost as the individual Rubin chips. So whereas NVL72 was originally slated to offer 28.8TB/second of networking bandwidth, that has been dialed up to 32.4TB/second (bidirectional). This means that for larger deployments that make heavy use of scale-out networking, more bandwidth (and ideally, more performance) is now available than NVIDIA first projected.
Past this, the rest of the figures for Vera Rubin NVL72 remain unchanged from the earlier specifications. Whether an NVL72 rack can hit quite the same level of AI performance with less memory and NVLink bandwidth as originally intended seems doubtful, but the GPU compute hardware (and its CPU counterpart) is shipping at spec.
NVIDIA Rubin HGX NVL8: Losing Some HBM4 Capacity as Well
Finally, separate from the specification changes to the base Rubin GPU and the NVL72 rack, NVIDIA has also revised its other products built from Rubin. This includes the Vera Rubin Superchip, the Vera Rubin NVL4, and the HGX Rubin NVL8 products. The last one is getting a special mention here because, on top of the Rubin spec changes, it is getting a further change of its own.
| NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 Specifications |  |  |  |  | 
|  | Preliminary | Shipping |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Inference | 400 PFLOPS | 400 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| NVFP4 Training | 280 PFLOPS | 270 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| FP8 Training | 140 PFLOPS | 130 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| TF32 | 16 PFLOPS | 16 PFLOPS |  |  | 
| GPU Memory | 2.3TB HBM4 | 2.0TB HBM4 |  |  | 
| GPU Memory Bandwidth | 176TB/sec | 130TB/sec |  |  | 
| NVLink Bandwidth (Scale Up) | 28.8TB/sec | 24TB/sec |  |  | 
| Networking Bandwidth (Scale Out) | 1.6TB/sec | 1.8TB/sec |  |  | 
On top of GPU memory bandwidth and NVLink bandwidth reductions, NVIDIA is also cutting back the amount of HBM4 memory available in NVL8 systems. These systems were originally set to come with 2.3TB of HBM4, but that is now down to a flat 2.0TB, losing 300GB (or 13%) of GPU memory.
NVIDIA’s preliminary figure would require each Rubin GPU in an NVL8 to be a full Rubin with its complete complement of 288GB of HBM4 available. However, a 2.0TB setup means each GPU needs only around 250GB of HBM4 available. That, in turn, requires only 7 of the GPU’s 8 HBM4 memory stacks.
Consequently, NVL8 is taking the biggest memory bandwidth hit of the entire Rubin family. Rather than losing just 11% of its memory bandwidth, it is losing 26%, or about 46TB/second. Each Rubin GPU would only have 250GB to 252GB of memory available, for 16.8TB/second of bandwidth per GPU.
Inference performance remains unchanged, at 400 PFLOPS for FP4, but FP4 training performance has been reduced from 280 PFLOPS to 270, and FP8 training has similarly been dialed down from 140 PFLOPS to 130. The 8-way Rubin systems do get the same network bandwidth improvement as the rest of the Rubin lineup. That figure has gone from 1.6TB/second to 1.8TB/second.
Finally, these changes affect both versions of the HGX NVL8, as well as DGX systems based on the NVL8 platform. Both the HGX Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + x86 CPU) and the HGX Vera Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + Vera) are subject to the same GPU changes.
Final Words
It seems NVIDIA has had to rein in its ambitions for the Rubin GPU to bring the product to market at the scale they are aiming for, dialing back both GPU HBM4 memory bandwidth and NVLink networking bandwidth. The full ramifications of these changes are unclear at this time since not all workloads are bottlenecked by memory or networking bandwidth in the same way. In some respects, it is academic, since these changes apply to all shipping Rubin hardware from day one. Still, there will be a lot of NVIDIA Rubin deployed over the next few quarters.
